📚 Reference Links

  • What a VPC is and what it contains — AWS: Amazon Virtual Private Cloud documentation

  • How DNS works inside the boundary — AWS: Understanding Amazon DNS

  • The same primitive, different topology — Google Cloud: VPC networks

  • The Azure equivalent — Microsoft Learn: Virtual networks and virtual machines in Azure

  • Bonus — AWS: Ensure internetwork traffic privacy in Amazon VPC

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What layer is a VPC? L3 — a private, isolated IP address space. Not a firewall, not a subnet, not a physical network.
Is a VPC regional or zonal? Regional on AWS; global on GCP. Subnets are zonal on AWS, regional on GCP.
What makes two VPCs unable to talk? Nothing is connected by default. Isolation is the default state, not a configured one.
How many IPs does AWS reserve per subnet? Five — network, VPC router, DNS, future use, broadcast. A /28 gives you 11 usable.
What is the .2 address in a VPC? The Amazon-provided DNS resolver, at VPC CIDR base + 2.

🪞 How to use this section: First pass — answer cold, mark misses. Read the note. Second pass — re-test only the misses. Third pass (day before) — full re-test.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

A VPC is your own private L3 network inside a cloud region — an IP address space that nobody else shares, with software-defined routing, addressing and DNS on top of hardware you do not see. The mental model that matters is that isolation is the default and every connection is something you built: a VPC cannot reach the internet, another VPC, or an on-premises network until you attach a gateway and write a route. Everything else in this section — subnets, NAT, peering, endpoints — is a specific answer to "how does traffic leave, and what is allowed to come back".

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

What is actually virtual about a Virtual Private Cloud?

🎯 Really testing: whether you understand it as software-defined networking or as a rented datacentre rack.

The addressing and the routing are virtual; the packets are real. Your instances get IPs from a CIDR block you chose, and they behave like a normal L3 network — ARP-like resolution, routing tables, a default gateway — but none of it is implemented by switches and routers you could point at. It is a distributed overlay: each hypervisor host runs a mapping service that encapsulates your packets and delivers them across the provider's physical fabric to the host holding the destination instance.

Two consequences follow. First, it is not a broadcast domain: promiscuous mode, ARP spoofing and sniffing a neighbour's traffic do not work, because the encapsulation layer will not deliver a frame to an instance that is not its destination — which is why traffic mirroring is a separate paid feature rather than something you achieve with a tap.

Second, the router is not a device you can fail. Every subnet has a virtual router at CIDR base + 1 implemented by the fabric, so there is no routing appliance to size, patch or lose. The flip side is that you cannot install anything on the path unless the provider gives you a hook, which is why gateway load balancers and endpoint services exist as products.

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

One large shared VPC, or many small ones?

📍 Seen in the wild: the opening question on any multi-team platform design.

🎯 Really testing: whether you weigh the connectivity cost of separation against the blast radius of sharing.

A single shared VPC is dramatically simpler at the network layer. Everything can reach everything without peering, endpoints or transit machinery; there is one CIDR to plan, one set of route tables, one place to attach a NAT gateway, and cross-service traffic stays free within an AZ. Isolation is done with security groups, which are identity-like — a security group can reference another security group as its source, which is a far better tool than IP ranges and is available only inside one VPC.

Many VPCs buy you hard boundaries: a misconfiguration in one cannot route to another, blast radius is bounded, and account-level separation maps cleanly onto team or environment ownership. The costs are all connectivity: peering is non-transitive and does not scale (Item 127), Transit Gateway costs per attachment and per GB (Item 128), each VPC needs its own NAT gateway or a shared-egress design, and every managed service you want privately needs endpoints in each VPC or a centralised endpoint pattern.

My default is one VPC per environment per region, per account — that boundary is the one you want to be uncrossable by accident — with teams separated by security group and IAM inside it rather than by more VPCs. Past that, the shared-VPC model scales: a networking account owns the VPC and shares subnets to workload accounts, giving account-level IAM isolation with single-VPC simplicity. The tipping point for real separation is a compliance boundary, not team count.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling (senior engineer testing depth)

What runs out first as a VPC grows?

📍 Seen in the wild: the follow-up whenever someone proposes one big VPC.

Address space, and it is the one thing you cannot fix in place. A VPC's primary CIDR is immutable; you can add secondary CIDR blocks, but you cannot resize or renumber the original, and every subnet inside it is likewise fixed at creation. A /16 looks generous until Kubernetes assigns a pod IP per pod from that space — with the AWS VPC CNI, pods take real VPC addresses, so a large EKS cluster consumes tens of thousands of them and a /16's 65,536 addresses stops being theoretical. Add five reserved addresses per subnet and the usual habit of over-provisioning subnets, and exhaustion arrives sooner than the arithmetic suggests.

It presents as pods stuck in ContainerCreating with "failed to assign an IP address", or an autoscaler that cannot launch instances in one AZ while another has room — a per-subnet failure, not a per-VPC one, which is why it looks like a scheduling bug. The signals are free-IP counts per subnet trending down (AvailableIpAddressCount, which is worth alerting on), ENI allocation failures in CNI logs, and capacity errors that name a specific subnet. The remedies in order of preference: add a secondary CIDR from 100.64.0.0/10 and put pods there, which is the standard EKS escape hatch; use prefix delegation so ENIs carry /28 blocks rather than individual addresses; and, structurally, plan the CIDR before the first terraform apply, because renumbering a live VPC means rebuilding it. The other limits — route table entries, security groups per ENI, ENIs per instance — are raisable quotas; address space is not.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design (architect-level)

Design the VPC topology for a multi-tenant AI product across three environments and two regions.

🎯 Really testing: whether you treat the network as something planned once and lived with, rather than something iterated on.

The dominating constraint is that CIDR decisions are permanent and everything else is reversible. So the design starts with an address plan, not a diagram: a single non-overlapping allocation across every environment and region — say a /12 for the organisation, carved into a /16 per region per environment — chosen so that any two VPCs can always be peered or attached to a Transit Gateway later without renumbering. Overlapping CIDRs between production and staging is the mistake that forecloses options you have not thought of yet, and it costs nothing to avoid on day one.

The topology: one VPC per environment per region in separate accounts, each with public subnets for load balancers, private subnets for workloads, and isolated subnets with no NAT route for databases. GPU inference nodes sit in the private tier with a secondary CIDR from carrier-grade NAT space for pod addressing, because that is where exhaustion bites. A network account holds a Transit Gateway per region with the regions peered — hub-and-spoke, not a peering mesh — and egress is centralised through a shared inspection VPC so per-tenant hostname allow-listing has one home.

The failure I would monitor first is AvailableIpAddressCount per subnet, alerting well before exhaustion, because the remedy has a long lead time and the symptom looks like something else entirely. Second is cross-AZ data transfer as a fraction of the bill, because a topology that spreads chatty services across AZs is charged per gigabyte in both directions and it is the line item that grows silently (Item 134). Third is the count of Transit Gateway attachments and route table entries against quota, since that is the number that decides whether the hub-and-spoke design survives the next ten teams.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Concept AWS GCP Azure Why the difference matters
The network VPC — regional VPC — global VNet — regional A GCP VPC spans regions, so "cross-region" needs no peering there
Subnet scope One AZ One region One region GCP subnets survive zone loss; AWS subnets must be replicated per AZ
Instance firewall Security group (stateful, on ENI) Firewall rules (stateful, on network + tags) NSG (stateful, on NIC or subnet) AWS's SG-references-SG is uniquely expressive
Subnet firewall NACL (stateless) (no direct equivalent) NSG on subnet Only AWS forces the stateless-rules conversation
Private managed-service access PrivateLink / VPC endpoints Private Service Connect Private Endpoint Same idea, three names
Transitive routing Not by default; needs Transit Gateway Within a VPC, yes (it's global) Needs peering + UDR or vWAN AWS's non-transitivity is the source of most topology complexity

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The four reserved facts about a VPC's address space. AWS reserves five addresses in every subnet: the network address, the VPC router at base+1, the DNS resolver at base+2, one reserved for future use at base+3, and the broadcast address at the top. So a /24 gives 251 usable addresses, not 256, and a /28 — the smallest AWS permits — gives 11. That five-address tax is trivial on large subnets and brutal on small ones, which is the arithmetic reason not to carve a VPC into many tiny subnets.

The VPC CIDR is immutable; subnets are immutable. You may add secondary CIDR blocks to a VPC and create new subnets, but you can never resize either. This is the single most consequential property in cloud networking: every other mistake in this section is a config change, and this one is a rebuild. Permitted primary block sizes on AWS run from /16 down to /28.

Address demand is set by the workload, not by the instance count. With the AWS VPC CNI, every Kubernetes pod holds a real VPC address, so demand is pods plus ENIs plus load balancer addresses plus endpoint addresses, not just servers. A cluster of 200 nodes running 30 pods each is 6,000 addresses before anything else — which is why the 100.64.0.0/10 secondary-CIDR pattern exists and why it should be planned rather than discovered.

Isolation is enforced at the mapping layer, not by rules. Two VPCs with identical CIDRs coexist happily because packets never leave their own overlay. That is why "the default is no connectivity" is a mechanism rather than a policy, and why every cross-VPC feature — peering, Transit Gateway, PrivateLink — is a separate product rather than a firewall rule.

7. Why It Matters in Production

The VPC is the boundary that decides what "private" means for the rest of your architecture. Every claim in a security review — the database is not reachable from the internet, tenant data never traverses a public path, egress is controlled — resolves to a route table and a security group inside a VPC. If the mental model is wrong, those claims are aspirational.

The observable that matters most is AvailableIpAddressCount per subnet, because it is the only VPC-level resource whose exhaustion cannot be fixed quickly. It is not on a default dashboard, it degrades silently for months, and it fails as a deployment error that looks like a scheduling problem.

The second is the shape of the bill. VPC networking is nearly free until traffic crosses a boundary, and then it is metered per gigabyte in ways that do not appear in any architecture diagram — cross-AZ, NAT processing, cross-region, internet egress. A topology decision made for elegance can multiply the network line item, which is why Item 134 exists as its own note.

8. Command / Config / Code Example

# The address plan is the design decision. Everything else is reversible.
resource "aws_vpc" "main" {
  cidr_block           = "10.20.0.0/16"   # IMMUTABLE. Chosen from an org-wide plan.
  enable_dns_support   = true             # the .2 resolver; off means no service discovery
  enable_dns_hostnames = true             # required for private hosted zones to resolve
}

# Secondary CIDR from carrier-grade NAT space - the standard EKS pod-IP escape hatch
resource "aws_vpc_ipv4_cidr_block_association" "pods" {
  vpc_id     = aws_vpc.main.id
  cidr_block = "100.64.0.0/16"            # not routable on the internet, not in RFC 1918
}

# Three tiers per AZ. Isolated tier gets NO route to NAT - that is what makes it isolated.
resource "aws_subnet" "private_a" {
  vpc_id            = aws_vpc.main.id
  cidr_block        = "10.20.16.0/20"     # 4091 usable after the 5 reserved
  availability_zone = "ap-south-1a"       # AWS subnets are ZONAL - one per AZ, always
}

9. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

An app instance at 10.20.16.42 in the private subnet above resolves and calls an internal service, then calls the internet.

📥 [1] app resolves orders.internal → queries 10.20.0.2 (VPC CIDR base + 2)
    │   the Amazon-provided resolver; requires enable_dns_support
    ▼
🔍 [2] private hosted zone answers 10.20.17.88 — never leaves the VPC  ....... ~0.4ms
    │
    ▼
🛣️ [3] packet to 10.20.17.88: route table's "10.20.0.0/16 → local" entry matches
    │   same VPC, same AZ → fabric delivers directly. No gateway. $0.
    ▼
✅ [4] response in ~0.5ms round trip (same-AZ)

📥 [5] app calls https://api.vendor.com — resolver returns a public IP
    │
    ▼
🛣️ [6] no local match → default route "0.0.0.0/0 → nat-0abc" (this is what
    │   makes the subnet "private": the default route points at NAT, not IGW)
    ▼
🔧 [7] NAT gateway rewrites source to its Elastic IP  .......... $0.045/GB processed
    │
    ▼
🌐 [8] IGW forwards to the internet  ........................... + internet egress $/GB
    ▼
✅ [9] return traffic: NAT's connection table maps it back to 10.20.16.42

  1. Step 2 never left the VPC, and that is the point of enable_dns_support. Turn it off and the .2 resolver disappears, private hosted zones stop resolving, and every VPC endpoint — which works by DNS — silently breaks. It is one boolean with a very large blast radius.

  2. Step 3 cost nothing because it stayed in one AZ. The local route is present in every route table and cannot be removed; it is what makes a VPC a single L3 domain. Had the destination been in AZ b, the same packet would have been charged cross-AZ data transfer in both directions (Item 134).

  3. Step 6 is the entire definition of "private subnet". There is no private attribute on an AWS subnet. A subnet is public if its route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to an internet gateway and private if it sends it to a NAT gateway — a route table entry, nothing more (Item 125).

  4. Step 7 is metered twice. NAT gateway charges per hour and per gigabyte processed, on top of the internet egress charge at step 8. Traffic to S3 or DynamoDB through NAT pays all of this for no reason, which is what gateway endpoints exist to eliminate (Item 129).

  5. Step 9 works because NAT is stateful. The return packet has no matching route in the private subnet's table — it arrives because the NAT gateway remembered the outbound flow. That statefulness is why a NAT gateway allows outbound-initiated traffic and nothing inbound, and it is the mechanism behind "private subnets can reach out but not be reached".

10. When TO Use This

  • Always, for anything running in a cloud region. There is no non-VPC option for modern compute; the question is only how many VPCs and how they are addressed.

  • A separate VPC per environment, at minimum. Production and non-production should be unable to route to each other by construction rather than by policy, and separate accounts plus separate VPCs is the cheapest way to make that true.

  • A shared VPC (subnets shared from a network account) when many teams need one address space. It gives account-level IAM isolation with single-VPC network simplicity, and it avoids n² peering.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Do not create a VPC per team or per service. Connectivity cost grows faster than isolation benefit: each one needs endpoints, egress, DNS and an attachment, and the transitive-routing problem arrives immediately. Security groups inside one VPC give finer isolation than a VPC boundary does, with none of the machinery.

  • Do not use the default VPC for anything real. Its subnets are all public, its sizing is not yours, and its existence in every region is an attack surface. Delete it or ignore it, and build an addressed one.

  • Do not pick a CIDR without an organisation-wide plan. 10.0.0.0/16 is the default that everyone accepts, which is exactly why two VPCs you will later need to connect both have it. Overlapping CIDRs cannot be peered, and the fix is a rebuild.

  • Scale limit worth naming: address space is the hard one. Route table entries, security group rules and ENIs are raisable quotas; the primary CIDR is immutable, and a live VPC cannot be renumbered.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "A public subnet means the instances in it have public IPs and a private subnet means they don't."

✅ Reality: The distinction is purely the route table's 0.0.0.0/0 target — internet gateway versus NAT gateway. An instance with a public IP in a subnet routed to a NAT gateway is unreachable from the internet, and an instance without a public IP in a subnet routed to an IGW cannot reach the internet either. The address and the route are independent facts.

❌ Misconception: "Two VPCs with the same CIDR will conflict."

✅ Reality: They coexist perfectly, because isolation is enforced by the encapsulation layer and their packets never meet. The conflict only appears the moment you try to connect them — peering and Transit Gateway both refuse overlapping ranges, which is why the CIDR plan has to anticipate connections you have not designed yet.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "A /16 is obviously enough address space."

✅ Reality: It is, until pods get VPC addresses. With the AWS VPC CNI every pod consumes a real IP, so a moderately sized EKS estate eats tens of thousands, and the five reserved addresses per subnet plus generous subnet sizing burn more. The 100.64.0.0/10 secondary-CIDR pattern exists precisely because so many teams discovered this after the VPC was immutable.

13. Tech Discussion Traps

Describing a VPC as "a private network in the cloud" and stopping. That is the marketing sentence. The version that survives a follow-up names the layer and the default: an L3 address space where nothing is connected until you attach a gateway and write a route — from which subnets, NAT, peering and endpoints all follow as answers to specific connectivity questions.

Not knowing which primitives are regional, zonal or global. AWS VPCs are regional and subnets zonal; GCP VPCs are global and subnets regional. Getting this wrong produces designs that cannot exist, and it is the fastest way to reveal that a cloud was learned from one provider's console.

Treating CIDR planning as an implementation detail. It is the one irreversible decision in the section, and a senior reviewer will probe it precisely because juniors treat it as boilerplate. Raising immutability unprompted signals that you have lived with a VPC rather than created one.

Stopping at the happy path. No account of what happens when an AZ is lost. Because AWS subnets are zonal, an AZ failure removes a subnet's worth of capacity and addresses, and a design with a single NAT gateway loses egress for every private subnet routed through it — a detail that only appears if you think past steady state.

14. Key Numbers & Benchmarks

Metric Value Context Source

15. Trade-offs & Performance Considerations

Dimension Trade-off
⏱️ Latency Same-AZ is ~0.5ms and cross-AZ is single-digit milliseconds — rarely the constraint; the AZ boundary costs money long before it costs time
💰 Cost The VPC itself is free; every boundary crossing is metered per GB. Topology choices are cost choices
🔒 Security / visibility Isolation is real and enforced below your control plane, but it stops routing, not a compromised identity inside the boundary
📈 Scale Address space is the only hard ceiling; everything else is a raisable quota. Pod-per-IP CNIs move demand by an order of magnitude
🔧 Ops complexity Each additional VPC multiplies endpoints, egress paths, DNS zones and attachments — connectivity cost grows faster than VPC count
🐛 Debuggability There is no wire to tap: flow logs and mirroring are the only visibility, and neither shows payloads by default

16. Real World Usage

The shared-VPC pattern is how large organisations avoid n² connectivity. One networking account owns the VPC and shares subnets into workload accounts, so teams get IAM isolation and their own resources while the network stays a single address space with one egress path and one set of endpoints. GCP's Shared VPC and AWS's RAM-based subnet sharing are the same idea reached independently.

The 100.64.0.0/10 pod-CIDR pattern is now standard practice on EKS. It is documented guidance rather than a trick, and its existence is the clearest evidence that VPC address exhaustion is a mainstream failure rather than an edge case.

17. Acronym Decoder

  • VPC — Virtual Private Cloud. The expansion is nearly self-explanatory, but each word carries a fact: Virtual (software-defined overlay, not physical kit), Private (an isolated address space, unreachable by default), Cloud (regional on AWS and Azure, global on GCP).

  • CIDR — Classless Inter-Domain Routing: the 10.0.0.0/16 notation, where the suffix is the number of fixed prefix bits. Covered fully in 02-ip-packets-routing/11-subnets-cidr.md.

19. System Design Application

How this concept appears in a system design tech discussion

Almost always as the frame rather than the subject: "draw your network" opens the design, and everything after it inherits the VPC decisions. The probes that follow are consistent — how did you size the CIDR, what makes that subnet private, what happens when an AZ fails, and how does this reach a managed service. The strongest answers state the address plan before the boxes, because that is the decision the reviewer knows is irreversible.

Topology diagram

Capacity / cost back-of-envelope

Scale Constraint Solution
10× (a few thousand pods) Subnet address exhaustion; five-address tax on small subnets Secondary CIDR from 100.64.0.0/10; prefix delegation on the CNI
100× (multi-account estate) Peering count becomes n(n−1)/2; endpoint duplication per VPC Transit Gateway hub; centralised endpoint and egress VPCs
1000× (multi-region, multi-org) Cross-region transfer and TGW per-GB charges dominate; route table quotas Region-local everything; replicate rather than call across regions; IPAM-managed address plan

Where this typically breaks at scale

  • 10×: free IPs per subnet. Fails as pods that will not schedule in one AZ while another has room.

  • 100×: connectivity machinery. Peerings, endpoints and DNS zones multiply per VPC until the topology is unmaintainable by hand.

  • Operational: an overlapping CIDR created by a team that did not know the plan, discovered only when two environments need to be connected — at which point one of them has to be rebuilt.

Monitoring & SLOs

  • AvailableIpAddressCount per subnet, alerting at 20% remaining. The only VPC resource whose exhaustion has a multi-week remedy.

  • Cross-AZ data transfer bytes, as a share of total network spend. Detects a topology that is spreading chatty traffic across zones (Item 134).

  • NAT gateway processed bytes per VPC. A rising figure with flat traffic usually means something that should be using a gateway endpoint is not.

  • VPC flow log rejects by security group and NACL. The first place a "why can't A reach B" incident resolves, and the only packet-level visibility this layer offers.

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
How many usable IPs in a /24 AWS subnet? 251. Five are reserved in every subnet, regardless of size.
How many usable in the smallest permitted subnet? /28 → 11 usable. /28 is the floor, /16 the ceiling.
Can you resize a subnet after creation? No. Neither a subnet nor the VPC's primary CIDR can be resized or renumbered.
How many subnets does a 3-AZ, 3-tier design need? 9 — every tier replicated per AZ, because AWS subnets are zonal.
Why avoid 10.0.0.0/16 as a default? Everyone picks it, so two VPCs you later need to peer will overlap and cannot be joined.

🪞 How to use this section: First pass — answer cold, mark misses. Read the note. Second pass — re-test only the misses. Third pass (day before) — full re-test.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

On AWS a subnet lives in exactly one availability zone, so a three-tier design across three AZs is nine subnets, not three. Each subnet is a slice of the VPC's CIDR, each loses five reserved addresses, and neither the subnet nor the VPC CIDR can ever be resized — which makes address planning the one irreversible decision in cloud networking. The planning rule that matters is to allocate from an organisation-wide scheme with no overlaps anywhere, because overlapping CIDRs cannot be peered, and the fix for a wrong plan is rebuilding the VPC.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

Why does a subnet map to an AZ, and what does that force?

🎯 Really testing: whether you know that AZ placement is a subnet property on AWS and a workload property on GCP.

An AWS availability zone is a distinct set of datacentres with independent power, cooling and networking, and a subnet is bound to exactly one of them at creation. That binding is what makes a subnet the unit of failure-domain placement: you do not choose an AZ for an instance directly, you choose a subnet, and the subnet chooses the AZ. Every multi-AZ design therefore replicates subnets — three tiers across three AZs is nine subnets, three route tables at minimum, and nine CIDR allocations to plan.

It also means an AZ failure removes a subnet's worth of capacity and addresses at once. An autoscaling group configured with three subnets can shift to the surviving two; one configured with one subnet cannot. And because each subnet has its own free-address pool, capacity headroom is per-AZ rather than pooled — you can have thousands of free addresses in the VPC and still fail to launch in the AZ you need.

GCP inverts this: subnets are regional, spanning every zone in the region, so a single subnet survives zone loss and address headroom is pooled across zones. That difference is worth naming explicitly, because a design that assumes one model reads as confused in the other.

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

Few large subnets or many small ones?

📍 Seen in the wild: the follow-up after you draw a three-tier VPC.

🎯 Really testing: whether you know what a subnet boundary actually buys, given that security groups do the isolation.

Many small subnets feel tidy and cost you real addresses: the five-address reservation is per subnet, so twenty /28 subnets waste a hundred addresses to give you 220 usable, and each one is an independent pool that can exhaust while its neighbours have room. They also multiply route tables and NACL associations, and NACLs are the stateless rule set nobody wants more of (Item 126).

Few large subnets pool addresses efficiently and keep the route table count small, at the cost of coarser blast radius — everything in one subnet shares a route table, so "this tier must not reach the internet" has to be a separate subnet, not a security group. That is the genuine reason to split: a subnet boundary exists to give something a different route table or a different AZ, and for nothing else. Isolation between workloads is a security group's job and security groups are strictly more expressive, because one can reference another as its source.

So my default is three tiers per AZ — public, private, isolated — sized generously, and no further subdivision unless a workload needs a genuinely different route (a subnet with no NAT route, a subnet routed through an inspection appliance). The exception that justifies more is Kubernetes with pod-per-IP networking, where dedicated large subnets on a secondary CIDR keep pod address churn away from everything else.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling (senior engineer testing depth)

You planned /24 subnets. The EKS cluster grows. What happens?

📍 Seen in the wild: the most common cloud-networking regret, and a good proxy for whether someone has operated a cluster.

A /24 gives 251 usable addresses, and with the AWS VPC CNI every pod holds one. Nodes consume addresses too — each ENI carries a primary address plus its share of pod addresses — so a subnet supporting 251 addresses might hold six nodes at 30 pods each before it is full. Scaling out then fails in one AZ while the other two still have room, because pools are per subnet.

It presents as pods stuck in ContainerCreating with "failed to assign an IP address to container", or a cluster autoscaler that launches nodes which never become ready, both correlated with one AZ. The signals are AvailableIpAddressCount on the affected subnet at zero, ENI allocation errors in the CNI daemonset logs, and — the tell that distinguishes it from a scheduling problem — capacity that exists in the other AZs and is not being used. The remedies, in order: attach a secondary VPC CIDR from 100.64.0.0/10 and create large pod subnets there, which is the documented EKS pattern and requires no rebuild; enable prefix delegation so each ENI is assigned a /28 rather than individual addresses, which multiplies pod density per node roughly sixteenfold; and, for new builds, size pod subnets at /19 or larger from the start. What you cannot do is grow the existing /24. That is the whole lesson: the remedy is always "add space elsewhere", never "make this bigger".

Tier 4 — Open-ended design (architect-level)

Design the address plan for an organisation running three environments across two regions, expecting to acquire companies.

🎯 Really testing: whether you plan for connections that do not exist yet, which is the only thing that makes a CIDR plan valuable.

The dominating constraint is that any two networks you might ever need to connect must not overlap — and since acquisitions and partner integrations are unpredictable, the plan has to leave room for networks you have never seen. That argues for allocating from a large, deliberately sparse block and reserving space rather than packing tightly.

Concretely: take 10.0.0.0/12 for the organisation's own workloads, which yields sixteen /16s. Assign by region and environment — 10.0.0.0/16 production ap-south-1, 10.1.0.0/16 production us-east-1, 10.16.0.0/16 staging ap-south-1, and so on — with a consistent, boring scheme where the octet encodes meaning. Inside each /16, carve /20s per AZ per tier so subnets are large enough that pod growth never forces a rebuild, and keep the upper half of each /16 unallocated as headroom. Reserve a separate range entirely — 10.128.0.0/12, say — for acquisitions and partner networks, and use 100.64.0.0/10 for pod address space so Kubernetes never competes with workload addressing at all. Deliberately avoid 10.0.0.0/16, 172.31.0.0/16 and 192.168.0.0/16 for anything that might be peered, because those are the defaults every acquired company will already be using.

The control that makes this survive contact with reality is IPAM: an address-management service or tool that owns allocation, so a team creating a VPC requests a block rather than choosing one. Without it the plan is a wiki page that is wrong within a quarter. The first thing I would monitor is allocation coverage — what fraction of the planned space is assigned — and the second is any VPC whose CIDR was created outside IPAM, because that is the one that will overlap. Both are cheap; the alternative is discovering the conflict on the day two businesses need to merge networks.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Subnet size Total IPs Usable (AWS) Typical use Watch out for
/28 16 11 Endpoint or appliance subnets only The 5-address tax is 31% of the block
/26 64 59 Small public subnets for load balancers ALB itself needs 8+ free per AZ
/24 256 251 The reflex default; fine for instances Far too small for pod-per-IP Kubernetes
/22 1,024 1,019 Comfortable app tier Reasonable floor for a mixed workload tier
/20 4,096 4,091 Recommended default for private tiers The size that stops you rebuilding later
/19 or larger 8,192+ 8,187+ Dedicated pod subnets on a secondary CIDR Pair with 100.64.0.0/10, not RFC 1918

5. Memory Hook (Story Form)

🪝 Hook

You are painting parking bays on a car park you can never repave.

📖 Story

You mark out bays before anyone arrives, and once the paint dries the lines are permanent — no widening a bay, no repainting the lot. Five spaces in every zone are taken by the attendant's hut, the entry barrier and the signage before a single car parks. Each zone has its own entrance, so a full zone stays full even when the one next door is empty. And the neighbouring car park you may one day knock a wall through to has numbered its bays too — if you both used the same numbers, the wall stays up.

🗺️ Story → Mechanism Mapping

  • Painted bays that cannot be repainted = subnet and VPC CIDRs are immutable after creation

  • Five spaces taken before anyone parks = the five reserved addresses in every AWS subnet

  • Each zone with its own entrance = subnets are per-AZ, and free-address pools do not pool across them

  • The neighbouring car park's numbering = overlapping CIDRs, which make peering impossible

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

Usable addresses = 2^(32−prefix) − 5. The subtraction is constant, which is why it dominates small blocks and vanishes on large ones: a /28 loses 31% of its space to reservations, a /20 loses 0.1%. This alone argues against carving a VPC into many small subnets.

Subnet count = tiers × AZs. Three tiers over three AZs is nine subnets on AWS, plus more if pods get their own. On GCP it is three, because subnets are regional. That multiplication is why AWS address plans run out faster than the raw VPC size suggests — you are not allocating three blocks, you are allocating nine, and each must be sized for its worst AZ rather than for average load.

Pod address demand is the term people omit. With the VPC CNI, demand ≈ nodes + pods + ENIs, and pods dominate. A 200-node cluster at 30 pods per node needs ~6,000 addresses; spread across three AZs that is 2,000 per subnet, which a /24 cannot hold and a /20 absorbs comfortably. Prefix delegation changes the arithmetic: instead of assigning secondary IPs one at a time, each ENI receives a /28 prefix, so a node's address capacity jumps roughly sixteenfold at the cost of allocating in blocks — more efficient per node, slightly wasteful per prefix.

Overlap arithmetic is binary. Two CIDRs either intersect or they do not, and if they intersect no peering, Transit Gateway attachment or VPN route will ever join them — the routing table cannot express two different destinations for the same prefix. There is no partial-credit mitigation short of NAT-ing one side, which is a permanent operational tax. This is why the plan matters more than the sizes.

7. Why It Matters in Production

This is the only decision in the section that cannot be undone with a config change. Everything else — routes, gateways, security groups, endpoints, even the load balancer type — can be changed in an afternoon. A wrong CIDR is a migration: new VPC, new subnets, every resource re-created, DNS cut over, and a maintenance window nobody wants.

The observable is AvailableIpAddressCount per subnet, and the reason it belongs on a dashboard is lead time. By the time it hits zero the remedy — a secondary CIDR, new subnets, node group replacement — takes days to weeks. Alerting at 20% remaining converts an outage into a planning ticket.

The second observable is subtler: capacity that exists in some AZs and not others. An autoscaler failing in one zone while another has headroom is almost always address exhaustion rather than instance-type scarcity, and knowing to check the subnet's free-IP count first saves an afternoon of looking at the wrong thing.

8. Command / Config / Code Example

locals {
  vpc_cidr  = "10.20.0.0/16"          # from the org-wide plan, NOT 10.0.0.0/16
  pod_cidr  = "100.64.0.0/16"         # carrier-grade NAT space: not RFC 1918, not routable
  azs       = ["ap-south-1a", "ap-south-1b", "ap-south-1c"]
}

# Three tiers x three AZs = nine subnets. Sized so pod growth never forces a rebuild.
resource "aws_subnet" "private" {
  for_each          = toset(local.azs)
  vpc_id            = aws_vpc.main.id
  availability_zone = each.value
  cidr_block        = cidrsubnet(local.vpc_cidr, 4, index(local.azs, each.value) + 1)
  # /16 + 4 bits = /20 => 4091 usable. The default that stops you rebuilding.
}

resource "aws_subnet" "pods" {                 # on the SECONDARY cidr, deliberately separate
  for_each          = toset(local.azs)
  vpc_id            = aws_vpc.main.id
  availability_zone = each.value
  cidr_block        = cidrsubnet(local.pod_cidr, 3, index(local.azs, each.value))
  # /16 + 3 bits = /19 => 8187 usable per AZ for pod addresses
  depends_on        = [aws_vpc_ipv4_cidr_block_association.pods]
}

9. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

The plan above, taken from creation to the first scaling event.

🎬 [1] VPC 10.20.0.0/16 created ................................ 65,536 addresses, IMMUTABLE
    │
    ▼
🧱 [2] nine subnets: 3 public /24, 3 private /20, 3 isolated /24
    │   allocated: 3x251 + 3x4091 + 3x251 = 13,779 usable
    │   remaining in the /16: ~50,000 unallocated headroom
    ▼
📦 [3] secondary CIDR 100.64.0.0/16 attached; three /19 pod subnets
    │   pod capacity: 3 x 8,187 = 24,561 — pods never touch the primary CIDR
    ▼
⚙️ [4] EKS scales to 200 nodes x 30 pods = 6,000 pod IPs
    │   AZ a subnet: 2,000 of 8,187 used → AvailableIpAddressCount 6,187 ✅
    ▼
📈 [5] traffic 4x. Autoscaler adds nodes; AZ a reaches 6,900 pod IPs
    │   alert fires at 20% remaining (1,637 free) → a planning ticket, not an outage
    ▼
🔧 [6] prefix delegation enabled: ENIs take /28 blocks instead of single IPs
    │   per-node pod density up ~16x; no new subnets needed
    ▼
✅ [7] had these been /24 private subnets, step 4 would have failed outright
       — 251 usable against a 2,000-address requirement, in one AZ, with no fix

  1. Step 1 is the irreversible one. Everything from step 2 onward is a Terraform change; step 1 is a rebuild. That asymmetry is the note.

  2. Step 2 deliberately leaves ~50,000 addresses unallocated. Headroom inside the /16 is free — you are not billed for unused address space — and it is the only thing that lets you add a tier or a fourth AZ later without touching the VPC.

  3. Step 3 is the decision that makes the design survive. Putting pods on a secondary, non-RFC-1918 CIDR means pod churn cannot exhaust workload addressing, and 100.64.0.0/10 will not collide with an acquired company's 10.x estate.

  4. Step 5 fired an alert, not an incident. AvailableIpAddressCount at 20% gives weeks of lead time; at zero the remedy takes days. The alert threshold is the entire value of the metric.

  5. Step 7 is the counterfactual worth stating out loud. The identical architecture with /24 private subnets fails at 200 nodes with no in-place fix — same diagram, same security groups, same everything, and a rebuild instead of a config change. Sizing is not a detail.

10. When TO Use This

  • Allocate from an organisation-wide plan before creating the first VPC. The plan costs an hour and removes an entire class of future migrations.

  • /20 as the default private-tier size. Large enough that instance and ENI growth never forces a rebuild, small enough that a /16 holds many of them.

  • A secondary CIDR from 100.64.0.0/10 for pod addressing. Documented practice on EKS, keeps Kubernetes churn out of workload space, and avoids collisions with anything using RFC 1918.

  • Three tiers per AZ — public, private, isolated — and no more. Split further only when a workload genuinely needs a different route table.

  • An IPAM service or tool to own allocation. A plan that teams request blocks from survives; a plan on a wiki does not.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Do not use 10.0.0.0/16, 172.31.0.0/16 or 192.168.0.0/16 for anything you might peer. They are the defaults everyone else picked, so a future partner, acquisition or vendor VPC will collide, and overlapping CIDRs cannot be joined at all.

  • Do not size subnets to current usage. Sizing is a bet on the maximum, and being wrong low is unfixable while being wrong high costs nothing — unallocated address space is free.

  • Do not carve many small subnets for isolation. The five-address tax is per subnet, pools stop being shared, and security groups already give finer isolation than a subnet boundary does.

  • Do not put pod addresses on the primary CIDR if you can avoid it. Pod churn is the most volatile address consumer you have, and mixing it with stable workload addressing means one bad deploy can exhaust the tier.

  • Scale limit worth naming: the ceiling is per-subnet and per-AZ, not per-VPC. A VPC with tens of thousands of free addresses can still fail to launch a single pod, and the metric that shows it is per-subnet.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "You can resize a subnet if you plan carefully."

✅ Reality: You cannot resize either a subnet or a VPC's primary CIDR. You can add secondary CIDR blocks and create new subnets alongside; the existing ones are fixed for their lifetime. Every remedy in this note is "allocate elsewhere", never "grow this".

❌ Misconception: "A /24 per subnet is a sensible default."

✅ Reality: It is the reflex inherited from on-premises networks where a subnet held physical machines. With pod-per-IP CNIs a /24 holds roughly six nodes' worth of pods, and it is the single most common cause of "we had to rebuild the VPC".

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "Unused address space is waste, so subnets should be sized close to need."

✅ Reality: Address space inside a VPC costs nothing — there is no charge for unallocated or unused IPs. Over-allocating is free and under-allocating is a rebuild, which makes this one of the few decisions with a genuinely asymmetric error cost. Generous sizing is the correct default, not sloppiness.

13. Tech Discussion Traps

Not stating that the decision is irreversible. Every other answer in this section describes something you can change. Naming immutability unprompted is the fastest way to show you have lived with a CIDR plan rather than authored one on a whiteboard.

Forgetting the AZ multiplication. Answering "three subnets" for a three-tier design reveals that subnet-per-AZ has not sunk in. Nine is the number, and the follow-up — what an AZ failure removes — only makes sense once you have said it.

Ignoring pod address demand. A design that sizes subnets for instances and then runs Kubernetes on the VPC CNI has undercounted by an order of magnitude. Bringing up pod-per-IP and the 100.64.0.0/10 pattern unprompted is a strong signal.

Quoting usable-address counts without the reservation. 256 for a /24 is the textbook answer and it is wrong here by five. Small numbers like this are exactly what a reviewer checks, because they are cheap to verify and reveal whether you have read the docs or the blog post.

Stopping before the connection you have not designed yet. The value of a CIDR plan is entirely about future peerings, acquisitions and partner links. An answer that optimises today's VPC in isolation has missed why anyone plans addresses at all.

14. Key Numbers & Benchmarks

Metric Value Context Source
Reserved IPs per AWS subnet 5 Constant regardless of subnet size AWS: Subnets for your VPC
Usable in /24 251 The number to quote, not 256 Derived: 2^8 − 5
Usable in /28 (smallest permitted) 11 The 5-address tax is 31% here AWS: Subnets for your VPC
Permitted subnet sizes /28 to /16 Same range as the VPC CIDR itself AWS: Subnets for your VPC
Usable in /20 (recommended private default) 4,091 Absorbs pod and ENI growth Derived: 2^12 − 5
Subnet AZ scope 1 AZ (AWS) / whole region (GCP) Drives the tiers × AZs multiplication AWS VPC docs; Google Cloud: Subnets

15. Trade-offs & Performance Considerations

Dimension Trade-off
⏱️ Latency Subnet layout has no latency cost inside an AZ; the meaningful boundary is the AZ, and it costs money before it costs milliseconds
💰 Cost Address space is free; the cost of a wrong plan is a migration, and the cost of a right one is an hour of planning
🔒 Security / visibility A subnet boundary buys a distinct route table and NACL — real controls, but coarser and less expressive than security groups
📈 Scale The ceiling is per-subnet and per-AZ; a VPC with capacity can still fail in one zone, which is why the metric must be per-subnet
🔧 Ops complexity Every extra subnet is another route table association, NACL and allocation to reason about — subdivide only for a routing reason
🐛 Debuggability Address exhaustion presents as a scheduling or capacity error, not a network one, so the diagnosis depends entirely on knowing to check free IPs

16. Real World Usage

The 100.64.0.0/10 pod-CIDR pattern is documented AWS guidance, not a hack. It exists because RFC 1918 space is scarce in large organisations and because pod addressing is the fastest-growing consumer in any Kubernetes estate; putting pods on carrier-grade NAT space keeps the two problems separate.

Cloud IPAM services exist because wiki-based plans fail. AWS IPAM, and equivalent tooling elsewhere, turn address allocation into a request-and-approve flow with enforced non-overlap. Organisations adopt them after the first painful collision, which is a reliable indicator that the failure is common.

Overlapping CIDRs are the standard blocker in acquisitions. Two companies each defaulted to 10.0.0.0/16, and joining their networks then requires NAT on one side permanently, or renumbering an entire estate. This is the concrete reason the "avoid the defaults" rule exists, and it is worth citing as the motivation rather than as a style preference.

17. Acronym Decoder

  • CIDR — Classless Inter-Domain Routing: 10.20.0.0/16 means 16 fixed prefix bits and 16 host bits. The name records that it replaced fixed class A/B/C boundaries with an arbitrary prefix length, which is exactly the flexibility this note depends on.

  • AZ — Availability Zone: one or more discrete datacentres with independent power, cooling and networking inside a region. The expansion matters here because "zone" is the failure domain a subnet is bound to.

  • Prefix delegation on the CNI — raises pod density per node instead of enlarging the address plan

📚 Reference Links

  • What an internet gateway is and the route it requires — AWS: Enable internet access for a VPC using an internet gateway

  • NAT gateway behaviour, limits and charges — AWS: NAT gateways

  • The reference private-subnet topology — AWS: Example: VPC with servers in private subnets and NAT

  • What it costs, per hour and per GB — AWS: Amazon VPC Pricing

  • Bonus — AWS: Using NAT Gateways with multiple Amazon VPCs at scale

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What makes a subnet public? Its route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to an internet gateway. That is the whole definition.
Where does a NAT gateway live? In a public subnet — it needs the IGW route itself to reach the internet.
Is an internet gateway a bottleneck? No. It is horizontally scaled, highly available and free. The NAT gateway is the metered part.
What does a NAT gateway charge? Per hour, plus per GB processed — on top of internet egress. Two meters, not one.
How many concurrent connections per NAT gateway? ~55,000 to a single destination IP:port, from the port range. Beyond that, add destinations or gateways.

🪞 How to use this section: First pass — answer cold, mark misses. Read the note. Second pass — re-test only the misses. Third pass (day before) — full re-test.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

An internet gateway is the VPC's attachment point to the public internet — horizontally scaled, highly available, and free. A subnet is "public" purely because its route table sends the default route there. A NAT gateway lets private subnets reach out without being reachable: it sits in a public subnet, rewrites the source address to its own Elastic IP, and remembers the flow so return traffic finds its way back. The thing to know is that it is metered twice — hourly plus per gigabyte processed — which stacks on top of internet egress, and it is the reason gateway endpoints for S3 exist.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

Why does an instance with a public IP in a private subnet still have no internet access?

🎯 Really testing: whether you separate addressing from routing, which is the core confusion in this topic.

Because an address is not a path. The internet gateway performs one-to-one NAT between an instance's private address and its public address, but it only sees traffic that is routed to it. If the subnet's route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to a NAT gateway — or nowhere at all — packets destined for the internet never reach the IGW, and the public address is inert.

The converse is equally true: an instance with no public address in an IGW-routed subnet also reaches nothing, because there is no public address to translate to. Internet access requires both facts — a public address and a route to the IGW — and neither implies the other.

This is why "public subnet" and "private subnet" are not attributes you can query on a subnet resource. They are shorthand for the target of the default route: IGW means public, NAT gateway means private, and no default route at all means isolated. Everything else in this note follows from that single distinction.

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

One NAT gateway or one per AZ?

📍 Seen in the wild: the classic cost-versus-availability question, and one people usually get wrong in one direction or the other.

🎯 Really testing: whether you can price both failure and cross-AZ transfer, rather than picking the cheap-sounding option.

A NAT gateway is a zonal resource. One gateway serving all three AZs means every private subnet routes its default through one zone: if that AZ fails, all egress fails everywhere, and in steady state two thirds of your outbound traffic crosses an AZ boundary and is charged cross-AZ data transfer in addition to NAT processing and internet egress. So the "cheap" option is frequently not cheaper — it trades an hourly charge for a per-gigabyte one, and the per-gigabyte one scales with traffic.

One gateway per AZ removes both problems: egress survives a zone failure, and traffic stays in-zone so no cross-AZ charge applies. The cost is the additional hourly charge per gateway, which is fixed and modest, plus the extra route tables — you need one route table per AZ, since the default route must point at that zone's gateway.

My rule: one per AZ in production, one shared in development. The break-even is low — a few hundred gigabytes a month of cross-AZ egress pays for the second gateway — and availability settles it for anything customer-facing. The genuinely different answer is a centralised egress VPC behind a Transit Gateway, which is what you do at ten-plus VPCs so filtering and cost live in one place; it trades per-VPC gateways for TGW attachment and per-GB charges, and only wins at scale (Item 128).

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling (senior engineer testing depth)

What runs out first on a NAT gateway?

📍 Seen in the wild: the follow-up on any high-fan-out egress design — scrapers, agent tool-calling, or a fleet polling one vendor API.

Ports to a single destination. A NAT gateway can support around 55,000 simultaneous connections to each unique destination IP and port, because that is the size of the source-port range it has available for that tuple. Bandwidth is rarely the limit — a gateway scales to tens of gigabits — and neither is total connection count. The limit is per-destination, which means the failure is triggered by concentration, not by volume: a thousand instances each holding fifty connections to one vendor endpoint is 50,000 connections to one IP:port, and that is the wall.

It presents as ErrorPortAllocation on the gateway's CloudWatch metrics and as connection timeouts or resets at the application, typically intermittent and correlated with peak concurrency rather than with total throughput — which is why it gets blamed on the vendor. IdleTimeoutCount rising alongside it is the confirmation, because idle flows hold their port allocation for the full 350-second idle timeout before release. The remedies in order: reuse connections with keepalive pooling so you stop opening one per request, which usually removes the problem outright; spread destinations, since the limit is per IP:port and a vendor behind multiple addresses gives you more headroom; add NAT gateways and split subnets across them, because each gateway has its own port range; and assign additional Elastic IPs where supported, since the range is per source address. Note that none of this is fixed by a bigger instance or more bandwidth — it is an addressing limit, not a capacity one.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design (architect-level)

Design the egress path for an AI platform whose agents call arbitrary third-party APIs, with per-tenant auditing.

📍 Seen in the wild: the agent-egress design, now a standard question on AI-platform rounds.

🎯 Really testing: whether you separate "reach the internet" from "control what is reached", which are two different hops.

The dominating constraint is that the destination set is chosen by a model at runtime, so no IP-based control can express the policy. A NAT gateway gives connectivity and an Elastic IP; it gives you no hostname visibility at all, because it operates on addresses. So the design needs two hops: a forward proxy doing hostname allow-listing and audit logging, and a NAT gateway behind it doing the actual address translation. Collapsing them is the mistake — flow logs from a NAT gateway can tell you an agent talked to 104.18.x.x and never that it talked to a competitor's API.

Concretely: agent workloads sit in private subnets with no default route to NAT at all. Their egress goes to an internal load balancer fronting a forward-proxy tier in its own subnets, which holds per-tenant hostname allow-lists and writes the audit log. Those proxy subnets route 0.0.0.0/0 to a NAT gateway per AZ, which routes to the IGW. S3, ECR, Secrets Manager and every other AWS service the workloads need get VPC endpoints, so that traffic never touches NAT — both because it is cheaper and because it keeps the proxy's log limited to genuinely external calls (Item 129).

The failure I would monitor first is ErrorPortAllocation on the NAT gateways, because agent traffic is exactly the bursty, high-concurrency, few-destinations shape that exhausts ports, and it presents as a vendor problem. Second is NAT processed bytes trending up against a flat external request count, which almost always means a new dependency is going out through NAT that should have an endpoint. Third is proxy allow-list denials by tenant, which is the security signal the whole design exists to produce — a spike there is either a misconfiguration or the thing you built this to catch.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Internet gateway NAT gateway Egress-only IGW (IPv6) Forward proxy
Direction Both ways Outbound-initiated only Outbound-initiated only Outbound-initiated only
Scope VPC-wide, regional Zonal — one per AZ for HA VPC-wide Wherever you run it
Requires public IP on instance Yes No — that is the point No (IPv6 is public by nature) No
Cost Free Hourly + per GB processed Free Your own compute
Sees hostnames No No No Yes — the reason it exists
Availability Managed, horizontally scaled Per-AZ; a zone failure kills its gateway Managed Yours to design
Scale limit None you will meet ~55,000 connections per destination IP:port None you will meet Ephemeral ports outbound
When you'd actually pick it Anything that must be reachable inbound Private workloads needing outbound access IPv6 workloads — free and unmetered You must control or audit what is reached

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The two translations are different. An internet gateway performs one-to-one NAT: it maps an instance's private address to its own public address, which is why a public IP on the instance is mandatory for the IGW path. A NAT gateway performs many-to-one NAT (port address translation): thousands of private addresses share one Elastic IP, distinguished by source port. That difference is why the IGW has no scale limit worth naming and the NAT gateway has a port ceiling.

The port ceiling is the arithmetic that matters. A NAT gateway supports roughly 55,000 simultaneous connections to each unique destination IP and port, drawn from the available source-port range for that tuple. The constraint is per-destination: 55,000 connections spread over ten vendor endpoints is comfortable, and 55,000 to one endpoint is the wall. Each additional Elastic IP, where supported, adds another range — which is the addressing-level reason more IPs help and more bandwidth does not.

Idle flows hold their ports. A NAT gateway's flow entries time out after 350 seconds of inactivity, and a flow occupies its port allocation for that entire window. So a workload that opens connections and abandons them without closing consumes ports for nearly six minutes each, which converts a modest request rate into port exhaustion. Explicit connection close and keepalive reuse are the two behaviours that keep the ceiling far away.

The meters stack. Traffic through a NAT gateway is charged per hour for the gateway plus per gigabyte processed, and then internet egress is charged separately on the same bytes. If the traffic also crosses an AZ to reach the gateway, cross-AZ transfer applies too — three or four line items on one flow. This is why S3 traffic through NAT is the canonical waste: a gateway endpoint removes the NAT processing charge and the egress charge in one change, at no cost (Item 129, Item 134).

7. Why It Matters in Production

Egress is where the private-subnet promise is actually delivered. "The database is not reachable from the internet" is not a firewall claim — it is the claim that no route table anywhere sends its subnet's default to an internet gateway. Getting this wrong is not a degradation; it is an exposure, and it is a two-line route table change away in either direction.

The observable that moves is NAT gateway processed bytes, and it is worth watching against a flat baseline of external requests. A rising ratio almost always means a dependency that should be using a VPC endpoint is going out through NAT — the single most common avoidable line item in a cloud bill, and one that no architecture diagram shows.

The second is ErrorPortAllocation, which is the metric that turns an intermittent, vendor-blaming outage into a five-minute diagnosis. It is not on a default dashboard, and its absence is why teams spend days on connection timeouts that were an addressing limit all along.

8. Command / Config / Code Example

# The IGW is free and VPC-wide. One per VPC, no sizing decision.
resource "aws_internet_gateway" "igw" { vpc_id = aws_vpc.main.id }

# NAT gateways are ZONAL. One per AZ, each in that AZ's PUBLIC subnet.
resource "aws_nat_gateway" "nat" {
  for_each      = aws_subnet.public                    # one per AZ, not one shared
  allocation_id = aws_eip.nat[each.key].id             # each EIP adds port headroom
  subnet_id     = each.value.id                        # MUST be a public subnet
}

# One private route table PER AZ, each pointing at its own zone's gateway.
resource "aws_route_table" "private" {
  for_each = aws_subnet.private
  vpc_id   = aws_vpc.main.id
  route {
    cidr_block     = "0.0.0.0/0"                       # this line is the whole definition
    nat_gateway_id = aws_nat_gateway.nat[each.key].id  # NAT => private. IGW => public.
  }
}

# The isolated tier gets NO default route at all - not "deny", simply no path.
resource "aws_route_table" "isolated" { vpc_id = aws_vpc.main.id }

9. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

The topology above, carrying 500 GB of vendor API traffic and 2 TB of S3 traffic in a month.

📥 [1] app 10.20.16.42 (private, AZ a) → api.vendor.com
    │   route table lookup: 0.0.0.0/0 → nat-az-a  ..................... same AZ, no cross-AZ charge
    ▼
🔧 [2] NAT gateway rewrites src to 52.x.x.x:PORT, records flow
    │   meter 1: NAT hourly | meter 2: $0.045/GB processed
    ▼
🌐 [3] IGW forwards; internet egress metered separately
    │   meter 3: internet data transfer out
    ▼
✅ [4] 500 GB of vendor traffic: NAT processing ~$22 + egress + hourly ~$32/gw

📥 [5] app 10.20.16.42 → s3://our-bucket (BEFORE endpoint)
    │   S3 resolves to a PUBLIC IP → same path as above
    ▼
💸 [6] 2 TB through NAT: ~$90 processing, for traffic that never left AWS
    │
    ▼
🔧 [7] add an S3 GATEWAY endpoint: a route table prefix-list entry, $0
    │   route table now: pl-xxxx (S3 prefix list) → vpce-xxxx
    ▼
✅ [8] AFTER: 2 TB never touches NAT. ~$90/month removed by one route entry.
    │
    ▼
⚠️ [9] separately: 1,200 pods x 45 conns to ONE vendor IP:443 = 54,000
       → ErrorPortAllocation begins. Fix is keepalive reuse, not bandwidth.

  1. Step 1 stayed in-zone because there is a gateway per AZ. With one shared gateway, two thirds of this traffic would have crossed an AZ boundary and been charged cross-AZ transfer on top of everything else — the hidden cost of the "cheaper" single-gateway design.

  2. Steps 2 and 3 are separate meters on the same bytes. NAT processing and internet egress are billed independently; quoting only one of them understates the cost of an egress-heavy design by roughly half.

  3. Step 6 is the classic waste. S3 traffic resolves to public addresses, so without an endpoint it takes the full NAT path and pays processing charges for traffic that never leaves the AWS network. Nothing in the architecture diagram shows this.

  4. Step 7 costs nothing. A gateway endpoint for S3 or DynamoDB is free — it is a prefix-list route, not a resource with an hourly charge — which makes it the highest-return single change available in this note.

  5. Step 9 is an addressing limit, not a capacity one. 54,000 connections to one destination IP and port approaches the ~55,000 ceiling regardless of throughput, and the gateway may be at 2% of its bandwidth when it starts failing. Connection reuse removes it; a bigger anything does not.

10. When TO Use This

  • Internet gateway for anything that must be reachable inbound. Public load balancers, bastion hosts where you still have them, and NAT gateways themselves.

  • NAT gateway per AZ for private workloads that need outbound access. The availability argument alone settles this for production, and the cross-AZ saving usually pays the extra hourly charge.

  • VPC endpoints for every AWS service you use. Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB are free and remove NAT charges outright; interface endpoints cost hourly but keep traffic off the internet path (Item 129).

  • A forward proxy in front of NAT when you must control or audit destinations. NAT sees addresses; only a proxy sees hostnames, and hostname policy is the only policy that works against a dynamic destination set.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Do not route S3, DynamoDB or other AWS-service traffic through NAT. It is pure waste: processing charges plus egress charges for traffic that stays inside AWS, removable by a free gateway endpoint.

  • Do not run one NAT gateway for a multi-AZ VPC in production. It makes a single zone a dependency for all egress and charges cross-AZ transfer on most of your traffic — worse availability and, at moderate volume, worse cost.

  • Do not treat a NAT gateway as an egress control. It permits every outbound destination and records only addresses. If your security review asks "what did this workload call", NAT flow logs cannot answer it.

  • Scale limit worth naming: ~55,000 connections per destination IP:port, with idle flows holding their ports for 350 seconds. It is triggered by concentration and idle connections, not by bandwidth, and no instance sizing affects it.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "The internet gateway is a bottleneck we need to size."

✅ Reality: It is horizontally scaled, redundant, imposes no bandwidth constraint and costs nothing. There is exactly one per VPC and no configuration beyond attaching it. Every scaling and cost concern in this topic belongs to the NAT gateway.

❌ Misconception: "A NAT gateway is a firewall — it blocks inbound traffic."

✅ Reality: It blocks inbound traffic only as a side effect of being stateful: there is no mapping for an unsolicited inbound packet, so it is dropped. It enforces no policy, allows every outbound destination, and is not a security control. Security groups and a forward proxy are.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "One NAT gateway is cheaper than three."

✅ Reality: Only in the hourly line item. A shared gateway means most private subnets send egress across an AZ boundary, which is charged per gigabyte in addition to NAT processing — so at moderate traffic the single gateway costs more, and it also makes one zone a dependency for all egress. The cheap-looking option is frequently both slower to recover and more expensive.

13. Tech Discussion Traps

Saying "public subnet" as if it were a property. It is a route table entry — 0.0.0.0/0 to an IGW — and saying so converts a memorised label into a mechanism you can reason from. Everything else in this note derives from it.

Conflating an address with a path. A public IP without an IGW route reaches nothing, and an IGW route without a public IP reaches nothing. Both facts are required, and treating them as one is the most common error on this topic.

Quoting NAT cost as a single number. It is hourly plus per-GB processed, and internet egress is charged on top. An answer with one meter has understated an egress-heavy design by around half, and cost is exactly where a reviewer will check your arithmetic.

Stopping at connectivity and never reaching control. Getting packets out is the easy half; knowing and constraining what they reached is the half a security review asks about. An answer that never distinguishes NAT from a proxy has answered only the first.

14. Key Numbers & Benchmarks

Metric Value Context Source
NAT gateway connections per destination IP:port ~55,000 simultaneous The real ceiling; per-destination, not total AWS: NAT gateways
NAT gateway idle flow timeout 350 seconds Idle connections hold their port for this long AWS: NAT gateways
NAT gateway charges Hourly and per GB processed Stacks on top of internet egress AWS: Amazon VPC Pricing
Gateway endpoint (S3, DynamoDB) cost $0 Free; removes NAT processing for that traffic entirely AWS: Amazon VPC Pricing
Internet gateway cost and limits Free, no bandwidth limit Horizontally scaled and redundant by design AWS: Enable internet access using an internet gateway
Egress-only internet gateway (IPv6) Free Outbound-only, no per-GB processing charge AWS: Amazon VPC Pricing

15. Trade-offs & Performance Considerations

Dimension Trade-off
⏱️ Latency A NAT gateway adds negligible latency in-zone; routing through another AZ's gateway adds a hop and a charge
💰 Cost Two meters on NAT plus internet egress plus possible cross-AZ; endpoints remove whole line items for free
🔒 Security / visibility NAT gives outbound-only reachability and address-level logs; hostname control and audit require a proxy hop
📈 Scale Bounded by ports per destination, not bandwidth — the limit is triggered by concentration and idle flows
🔧 Ops complexity Per-AZ gateways mean per-AZ route tables; centralised egress trades that for Transit Gateway machinery
🐛 Debuggability Flow logs show addresses and ports only; "which hostname did we call" is unanswerable at this layer by construction

16. Real World Usage

Centralised egress VPCs are the standard large-organisation pattern. Rather than a NAT gateway per AZ per VPC across dozens of VPCs, one egress VPC behind a Transit Gateway holds the NAT gateways and the inspection tier, so cost and policy live in one place. AWS documents this explicitly as the multi-VPC-at-scale approach, and the trade is TGW attachment and per-GB charges against gateway sprawl.

S3 gateway endpoints are the most reliably recommended cost fix in AWS. They are free, require one route table entry, and remove NAT processing charges for what is often the largest single traffic flow in a data-heavy account. That a free one-line change is this impactful is itself the argument for auditing what goes through NAT.

17. Acronym Decoder

  • NAT — Network Address Translation: rewriting addresses (and, for a NAT gateway, ports) as packets cross a boundary. The expansion is the mechanism: a NAT gateway does many-to-one translation using ports, which is why it has a port ceiling; an internet gateway does one-to-one translation, which is why it does not.

  • IGW / EIGW — Internet Gateway and Egress-Only Internet Gateway. The second name is the whole specification: outbound-initiated only, for IPv6.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)

  • 122-vpc-mental-model.md — the boundary this note is about crossing

  • 02-ip-packets-routing/15-nat.md — NAT as a general mechanism, before its cloud form

  • 123-subnets-azs-cidr-planning.md — why a NAT gateway is zonal and what that forces

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

  • 125-route-tables.md — the mechanism that decides which gateway a packet reaches

  • 129-privatelink-vpc-endpoints.md — how to avoid this path entirely for AWS services

  • 134-egress-cost-data-transfer.md — the full cost picture this note only samples

🔀 Alternatives / Competing approaches

  • VPC endpoints — for AWS services, strictly better than NAT on both cost and exposure (Item 129)

  • Egress-only internet gateway — same semantics for IPv6, with no per-GB charge

  • NAT instance — the self-managed predecessor; cheaper at tiny scale, an availability and maintenance liability otherwise

  • Centralised egress VPC — one NAT tier for many VPCs, behind a Transit Gateway (Item 128)

🧩 Composes with (used together in real systems)

  • Forward proxy — the hop that adds hostname policy and audit above NAT (Section 11, Item 104)

  • Security groups — what decides whether the outbound connection is allowed at all (Item 126)

  • Flow logs — the only visibility this layer offers, and address-level only

19. System Design Application

How this concept appears in a system design tech discussion

Typically as the probe that follows your network diagram: "how does that private service reach the vendor API, and what does it cost?" The strong answer names the route table as the mechanism, places NAT gateways per AZ, removes AWS-service traffic to endpoints unprompted, and separates connectivity from control by adding a proxy where auditing is required. The follow-up is almost always cost or the port ceiling.

Topology diagram

Capacity / cost back-of-envelope

Scale Constraint Solution
10× (a few TB/month egress) NAT processing charges become visible; AWS-service traffic dominates Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB; interface endpoints for the rest
100× (high-concurrency agent traffic) ErrorPortAllocation from connection concentration on few destinations Keepalive pooling first; additional EIPs and gateways; spread destinations
1000× (dozens of VPCs, multi-region) NAT gateway sprawl; policy scattered across accounts Centralised egress VPC behind Transit Gateway; one inspection and audit tier

Where this typically breaks at scale

  • 10×: the bill. NAT processing on traffic that had a free endpoint available, invisible on every diagram.

  • 100×: port allocation to a concentrated destination set — presents as vendor flakiness, correlated with concurrency rather than volume.

  • Operational: a route table edited to add a route, with the default 0.0.0.0/0 target changed from NAT to IGW. Nothing errors; a private subnet quietly becomes public.

Monitoring & SLOs

  • ErrorPortAllocation on every NAT gateway, alerting on any non-zero value. It is the metric that turns a multi-day vendor investigation into a five-minute diagnosis.

  • NAT processed bytes per gateway, against external request count. A rising ratio means something with an available endpoint is going out through NAT.

  • IdleTimeoutCount. Rising values mean connections are being abandoned rather than closed, which is the leading indicator for port exhaustion.

  • An alert on any route table whose 0.0.0.0/0 target changes. This is a config-drift check rather than a metric, and it is the control that keeps "private" true.
