📚 Reference Links

  • Route table concepts, the local route and priority — AWS: Route table concepts

  • Association rules and the main route table — AWS: Configure route tables

  • Worked topologies for each target type — AWS: Example routing options

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Which route wins when two match? The most specific prefix — longest-prefix match. 10.0.1.0/24 beats 0.0.0.0/0.
Can you delete the local route? No. Every route table has it, it covers the VPC CIDR, and it always wins inside the VPC.
What happens to a subnet with no explicit association? It uses the VPC's main route table — which is why an unassociated subnet silently inherits behaviour.
How many route tables does a 3-AZ private tier need? Three, if each AZ has its own NAT gateway. One per distinct default-route target.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

A route table is the actual mechanism behind every "public" and "private" label in cloud networking. It is a list of destination prefixes and targets, evaluated by longest-prefix match, associated with one or more subnets. Every table contains an undeletable local route covering the VPC CIDR, which is why anything inside the VPC is always reachable. Everything else — internet access, NAT, peering, endpoints, Transit Gateway — is an entry someone added. A subnet with no explicit association silently falls back to the main route table, which is how subnets accidentally become public.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

How does the VPC router choose between overlapping routes?

Longest-prefix match, the same rule as any IP router: the entry whose prefix covers the destination with the most fixed bits wins, regardless of the order it appears in the table. So a table containing 0.0.0.0/0 → nat-gw, 10.20.0.0/16 → local and 10.30.0.0/16 → pcx-peering sends traffic for 10.30.5.7 over the peering connection, traffic for 10.20.5.7 locally, and everything else to NAT. There is no metric, no cost and no ordering to configure — specificity is the entire algorithm.

Two consequences follow. The local route always wins for in-VPC destinations because nothing can be more specific than the VPC CIDR entry for addresses inside it, and it cannot be deleted — which is why you cannot force intra-VPC traffic through an inspection appliance by routing alone, and why doing so requires more specific routes for individual subnets or a different mechanism entirely. Second, prefix lists (used by gateway endpoints and managed by AWS) participate in the same matching, so an S3 gateway endpoint works by inserting a highly specific set of prefixes that outrank the default route.

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

One route table shared across subnets, or one per subnet?

🎯 Really testing: whether you know that a route table is a shared object with an association fan-out, and what that means for blast radius.

Sharing is the norm and it is correct when the subnets genuinely need identical routing: three isolated subnets with no default route can share one table, and so can three public subnets pointing at the same internet gateway. Fewer tables means fewer places to make a change and fewer to audit.

Separate tables become necessary the moment routing differs, and the most common driver is per-AZ NAT gateways: each private subnet must send 0.0.0.0/0 to its own zone's gateway, so three AZs means three private route tables, no matter how identical the rest of their entries are. The other driver is blast radius — a route table is a shared mutable object, and an entry added for one subnet's needs applies instantly to every subnet associated with it. Editing a table associated with fifteen subnets to unblock one of them is a change with fourteen unintended participants.

My rule is one table per distinct routing intent, not per subnet and not per tier: public (IGW), private-per-AZ (that zone's NAT), isolated (no default route), and one more for anything that must traverse an inspection path. Beyond that, additional tables are duplication that will drift.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Target type What it means Typical entry Makes the subnet
local The VPC's own CIDR — implicit, undeletable 10.20.0.0/16 → local Always present
Internet gateway Direct internet path, both directions 0.0.0.0/0 → igw-xxx Public
NAT gateway Outbound-only via address translation 0.0.0.0/0 → nat-xxx Private
(no default route) No path off the VPC at all — Isolated
Peering connection One other VPC's CIDR, non-transitively 10.30.0.0/16 → pcx-xxx Peered
Transit gateway Many networks via a hub 10.0.0.0/8 → tgw-xxx Hub-attached
Gateway endpoint An AWS service's prefix list pl-xxxx → vpce-xxx Endpoint-routed
Virtual private gateway On-premises networks over VPN or Direct Connect 192.168.0.0/16 → vgw-xxx Hybrid

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The evaluation is stateless and per-packet, with no ordering and no cost metric — specificity alone decides. That makes route tables easy to reason about and easy to change destructively: adding a more specific prefix silently redirects a slice of traffic that was previously covered by a broader entry, with no warning and no error.

The association model is where the surprises live. A route table is associated with zero or more subnets, and a subnet with no explicit association uses the VPC's main route table. If the main table has a 0.0.0.0/0 → igw entry — which the default VPC's does — then any subnet created without an explicit association is public the moment it exists. The defensive practice is to leave the main route table empty except for local and to associate every subnet explicitly, so that a forgotten association fails closed rather than open.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Do not rely on the main route table's contents. Keep it empty apart from local, so an unassociated subnet is isolated rather than accidentally public. This is a one-time change that removes an entire class of exposure.

  • Do not try to force intra-VPC traffic through an appliance with routes. The local route always wins for in-VPC destinations and cannot be removed; inspection between subnets in the same VPC needs more specific per-subnet routes or a different design.

  • Do not share one route table across AZs when NAT gateways are per-AZ. Every subnet in the shared table would send egress to one zone's gateway, reintroducing both the cross-AZ charge and the single-zone dependency you added the extra gateways to remove.

  • Do not edit a widely-associated route table to fix one subnet. The change applies instantly to every associated subnet, with no staged rollout and no dry run.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "Routes are evaluated top to bottom, like firewall rules."

✅ Reality: There is no order. Longest-prefix match selects the most specific entry regardless of position, which is why adding a /32 silently overrides a /16 and why route tables cannot express "try this, then that".

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "Deleting a subnet's route table association is a safe way to cut it off."

✅ Reality: It falls back to the VPC's main route table, which may well have an internet gateway route. Removing an association does not isolate a subnet — it hands it whatever the main table says, which is the opposite of the intent.

📚 Reference Links

  • Security group semantics and defaults — AWS: Control traffic to your AWS resources using security groups

  • NACL rule evaluation and the stateless consequence — AWS: Control subnet traffic with network access control lists

  • How "stateful" is actually implemented, and where it stops — AWS: Amazon EC2 security group connection tracking

  • The Azure model, which merges the two levels — Microsoft Learn: Azure network security groups overview

  • Bonus — AWS: Example: Control access to instances in a subnet

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The one-line difference? SG: stateful, on the ENI, allow-only. NACL: stateless, on the subnet, allow and deny, ordered.
Why do NACLs need ephemeral port rules? Stateless — the return traffic is a separate decision, arriving on ports 1024–65535.
What can an SG source be that a NACL's cannot? Another security group. Identity-like, not IP-like — the single most useful feature here.
Default SG vs default NACL behaviour? Default SG: deny all inbound, allow all outbound. Default NACL: allow all both ways.
How are NACL rules evaluated? In rule-number order, first match wins, then an implicit deny. Unlike route tables.

🪞 How to use this section: First pass — answer cold, mark misses. Read the note. Second pass — re-test only the misses. Third pass (day before) — full re-test.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

A security group is a stateful allow-list attached to a network interface: allow the inbound connection and the return traffic is automatically permitted, because the connection is tracked. A network ACL is a stateless, ordered rule list attached to a subnet, it supports explicit deny, and it evaluates each direction independently — so allowing inbound HTTPS without also allowing outbound ephemeral ports produces a connection that arrives and never answers. In practice security groups do the work, because a security group can name another security group as its source, and NACLs are reserved for coarse subnet-wide denies.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

What does "stateful" actually mean here, mechanically?

🎯 Really testing: whether you know there is a connection-tracking table, with entries and limits, rather than a magic property.

The security group implementation maintains a connection tracking table for flows through each network interface. When an inbound packet is allowed by a rule, an entry is created recording the five-tuple; return packets matching that entry are permitted without consulting any rule, and the entry is removed when the connection closes or times out. That is the whole of "stateful" — a table, with a finite size and idle timeouts.

Two consequences that come up. First, changing a security group rule affects existing tracked connections: if you remove an allow rule, tracked flows that were permitted under it are terminated rather than grandfathered. That is a genuine improvement over a stateless model, and it surprises people who expect existing sessions to survive a rule change.

Second, not every flow is tracked. Traffic permitted by a rule allowing all traffic in both directions can be untracked, saving table capacity. That matters at scale: the table is a finite per-instance resource, and a very high-connection instance can exhaust it — the symptom being dropped connections that every rule permits.

A NACL has none of this. It evaluates each packet against an ordered list in one direction with no memory, which is why every allowed inbound flow needs a matching outbound rule for its return traffic.

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

When would you actually use a NACL?

📍 Seen in the wild: the follow-up after you say "security groups do the work".

🎯 Really testing: whether you know the one capability NACLs have that security groups lack, and whether you can resist using it for everything else.

Security groups cannot express deny. They are allow-only, and the effective policy is the union of every group attached to an interface — so there is no way to say "everything in this subnet, except this range" or "block this address regardless of what any group permits". A NACL can, and that is its only genuinely distinct capability.

So the legitimate uses are narrow and coarse: blocking a specific hostile CIDR at the subnet edge during an incident, enforcing a subnet-wide guarantee that survives whatever security groups individual teams attach, and satisfying a compliance requirement for a defence-in-depth layer at a different level. All of those are broad strokes applied to a whole subnet, which matches what a NACL is good at.

What makes NACLs wrong for routine work is statelessness plus ordering. Every allow needs a companion return rule, ephemeral ranges must be opened wide because you cannot predict the response port, and numbering means an inserted rule can silently shadow a later one. The result is hard to read, easy to break, and — because a whole ephemeral range is open anyway — often less restrictive than it looks.

My position: security groups for everything, referencing each other rather than IP ranges; NACLs left at their permissive default except for a small number of explicit denies, documented, at the subnet boundary. Reaching for a NACL to implement ordinary service-to-service policy is a design smell.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling (senior engineer testing depth)

You add a NACL to a subnet that is working fine. Half your traffic breaks. Why?

📍 Seen in the wild: the most common self-inflicted outage in this topic.

Because the return path is a separate decision and you only wrote the forward rules. A NACL allowing inbound 443 and outbound 443 looks symmetric and correct, and it breaks every client. An inbound HTTPS request arrives at port 443 from a client's ephemeral port; the response goes outbound to that ephemeral port, not from-443-to-443 in the sense the rules imply — so the outbound rule must allow destination ports 1024–65535, not 443. The mirror problem applies to outbound-initiated flows: allowing outbound 443 to a vendor requires an inbound rule permitting ports 1024–65535 for the responses.

It presents as connections that establish and hang, or as one direction working while the other does not — and crucially, as a failure that appears only for some traffic, because anything already tracked at the security group layer is unaffected while new NACL-blocked flows fail. The signals are REJECT entries in VPC flow logs with the NACL as the cause, TCP retransmissions at the client, and the tell that separates it from a security group problem: the SG shows an ACCEPT and the flow still fails, because both layers must permit the packet and flow logs record each decision.

The remedies are to write the ephemeral-range companion rules for every allow, to remember that NACL rule numbers determine evaluation order so inserted rules can shadow existing ones, and — the structural fix — not to use NACLs for this at all. Additionally, the rule count per NACL is quota-limited and evaluated per packet, so a large hand-maintained rule list is both a performance and a correctness liability.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design (architect-level)

Design the network security posture for a multi-tenant platform where tenant workloads must not reach each other.

🎯 Really testing: whether you reach for identity-based grouping rather than IP ranges, and whether you know where network controls stop.

The dominating constraint is that tenant workloads are dynamic — pods and instances come and go, addresses are recycled — so any policy written in IP ranges is wrong within minutes. That rules out NACLs for the primary control immediately: they match on CIDR and nothing else. Security groups can reference other security groups as sources, which means the policy is expressed as "the app tier may reach the database tier" and remains true as membership changes. That is the mechanism the whole design should rest on.

Concretely: one security group per tier per tenant, with rules that reference groups rather than ranges; a database group whose only inbound rule permits port 5432 from the corresponding app group; an app group whose only inbound rule permits 8080 from the load balancer's group. NACLs stay at their default-allow, with the single exception of a documented deny list at the subnet edge for known-bad ranges, so that the layer exists for defence in depth without becoming the place policy lives. Inside Kubernetes, security groups stop at the node boundary for most CNIs, so pod-to-pod isolation needs NetworkPolicy or a mesh's authorization policy as a second, complementary layer — the network control plane does not extend inside a node by default, and a design that assumes it does has a gap it cannot see.

The failure I would monitor first is flow log REJECT volume by security group, because a spike is either an attack or — far more often — a legitimate change that nobody updated a rule for, and both need to be seen quickly. Second is security group rule count per interface against quota, which is the number that quietly caps how far the referencing design scales before it needs restructuring. Third is any NACL whose rules deviate from the documented baseline, since an undocumented NACL edit is the most likely cause of an outage nobody can explain.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Dimension Security group Network ACL Which matters when
Attaches to Network interface (ENI) Subnet SG follows the workload; NACL follows the address range
State Stateful — return traffic auto-allowed Stateless — each direction decided separately The single biggest source of NACL bugs
Rule types Allow only Allow and deny The one thing only a NACL can do
Evaluation All rules; union of all attached groups Rule-number order, first match wins An inserted NACL rule can shadow a later one
Source can be CIDR, prefix list, another security group CIDR only SG-references-SG is why SGs win for dynamic workloads
Default (custom VPC) Deny all in, allow all out Allow all both directions A new NACL denies everything until you write rules
Ephemeral ports Never needed Required on the return direction 1024–65535, and the reason NACLs read as permissive
Applies to traffic between instances in the same subnet Yes No — NACLs only see traffic crossing the subnet boundary A NACL cannot isolate two instances in one subnet
When you'd actually pick it Everything: service-to-service policy, dynamic membership Coarse subnet-wide denies, incident blocking, compliance layering —

5. Memory Hook (Story Form)

🪝 Hook

The doorman remembers you; the gate guard reads a list.

📖 Story

A doorman stands at each apartment door. When he lets a visitor in, he remembers them, so when they walk out he opens the door without checking anything. He has no list of people to turn away — only a list of who may enter, and if any of his several lists says yes, they come in. Down at the estate's boundary gate, a different guard checks a numbered rulebook, top to bottom, acting on the first line that matches, and he can refuse people as well as admit them. He has no memory at all: the visitor who walked in past him needs a separate rule to walk back out.

🗺️ Story → Mechanism Mapping

  • The doorman at each door = a security group on an ENI; the gate guard at the boundary = a NACL on the subnet

  • Remembering the visitor = connection tracking, which is what "stateful" means

  • Only a list of who may enter = security groups are allow-only, and the union of all attached groups

  • The numbered rulebook, first line that matches = NACL rule-number ordering, first match wins

  • Needing a separate rule to walk back out = the ephemeral-port return rule every NACL allow requires

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

Both layers must permit a packet, and they decide independently. Inbound traffic hits the NACL first and the security group second; outbound is the reverse. A flow log entry records the decision, which is why an ACCEPT at the security group with the connection still failing points squarely at the NACL.

The effective security group policy is a union. Attaching three groups to an interface yields the union of their allow rules — there is no precedence, no ordering and no way for one group to override another, because none of them can deny. This is what makes security groups composable: a "base" group with common rules plus a service-specific group is a safe pattern, since adding a group can only widen access, never narrow it.

NACL evaluation is ordered and terminates on first match. Rules carry numbers, evaluation ascends, and the first matching rule decides — after which nothing else is consulted. An allow at rule 100 makes a deny at rule 200 unreachable for that traffic, which is the opposite of the security group model and the reason NACL rule sets are hard to reason about as they grow. There is an implicit deny at the end, so a newly created custom NACL blocks everything until rules are written.

The ephemeral range is the arithmetic to remember. Return traffic arrives on a client-chosen source port, and Linux's default range is 32768–60999 while the conventionally-quoted safe range is 1024–65535. Because the responding side cannot know which port a given client picked, a stateless rule set must open the whole range — which is why a NACL that looks locked down is admitting a very wide port range in one direction by necessity.

NACLs do not see intra-subnet traffic. A NACL is evaluated at the subnet boundary, so two instances in the same subnet communicate without any NACL involvement at all. Any isolation between them must come from security groups — a fact that quietly invalidates designs which place "sensitive" and "general" workloads in one subnet and expect the NACL to separate them.

7. Why It Matters in Production

This is the layer where "who can talk to whom" is actually true, and it is the layer an auditor will read. Every architectural claim about isolation — tenants separated, the database unreachable from the app tier's public subnet, admin ports restricted — resolves to a security group rule or it is not enforced at all.

The observable is flow log REJECT volume, broken down by security group and by NACL. A spike is either something malicious or, far more often, a deploy whose new component nobody wrote a rule for; both need to surface in minutes rather than in a support ticket. The breakdown matters because it tells you which layer denied, and that determines whether you are looking at a workload-scoped or a subnet-scoped problem.

The second is security group rule count per interface against quota. The referencing design that makes security groups powerful also multiplies rules, and the quota is the ceiling that eventually forces a restructure — better discovered on a dashboard than during a deploy.

8. Command / Config / Code Example

# Security groups referencing each other - membership can change freely, policy stays true
resource "aws_security_group" "app" {
  vpc_id = aws_vpc.main.id
  ingress {
    from_port       = 8080
    to_port         = 8080
    protocol        = "tcp"
    security_groups = [aws_security_group.alb.id]   # NOT a CIDR: identity, not address
  }
  egress { from_port = 0, to_port = 0, protocol = "-1", cidr_blocks = ["0.0.0.0/0"] }
}

resource "aws_security_group" "db" {
  vpc_id = aws_vpc.main.id
  ingress {
    from_port       = 5432
    to_port         = 5432
    protocol        = "tcp"
    security_groups = [aws_security_group.app.id]   # only the app tier, whatever its IPs are
  }
  # no egress rule needed for replies - stateful
}

# NACL: coarse deny only. Note the ephemeral-range rule that statelessness forces.
resource "aws_network_acl_rule" "block_bad_actor" {
  network_acl_id = aws_network_acl.public.id
  rule_number    = 50            # LOW number - evaluated before the permissive allows
  egress         = false
  protocol       = "-1"
  rule_action    = "deny"
  cidr_block     = "198.51.100.0/24"
}

resource "aws_network_acl_rule" "outbound_ephemeral" {
  network_acl_id = aws_network_acl.public.id
  rule_number    = 200
  egress         = true          # WITHOUT this, every inbound request hangs unanswered
  protocol       = "tcp"
  rule_action    = "allow"
  from_port      = 1024          # responses go to the CLIENT's ephemeral port,
  to_port        = 65535         # which you cannot predict - so the range must be open
  cidr_block     = "0.0.0.0/0"
}

9. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

A client calls the app tier through the load balancer, with the configuration above.

📥 [1] client 203.0.113.9:52341 → ALB :443
    │   public subnet NACL: rule 50 deny 198.51.100.0/24 → no match
    │                       rule 100 allow tcp 443 → MATCH, evaluation STOPS  ✅
    ▼
🛡️ [2] ALB security group: allow 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 → ACCEPT
    │   connection tracking entry created for the 5-tuple
    ▼
⚙️ [3] ALB → app 10.20.16.42:8080, source = ALB's ENI (sg-alb)
    │   app SG: allow 8080 from sg-alb → MATCH by GROUP, not by IP  ✅
    │   (the app scaled from 3 to 30 instances this morning; no rule changed)
    ▼
💾 [4] app → db 10.20.64.10:5432, source sg-app
    │   db SG: allow 5432 from sg-app → ACCEPT
    │   private subnet NACL: default allow-all → passes
    ▼
🔙 [5] db reply: no egress rule consulted — tracked flow, auto-permitted
    │
    ▼
🔙 [6] ALB reply to client → outbound to 203.0.113.9:52341
    │   public NACL outbound: rule 200 allow tcp 1024-65535 → MATCH  ✅
    │   ⚠️ WITHOUT rule 200: SG says ACCEPT, NACL says REJECT, connection hangs
    ▼
✅ [7] 200 OK

  1. Step 1 stopped at the first match. NACL rule 50's deny was evaluated before rule 100's allow because of the numbering — which is exactly why a deny must carry a low rule number. Placed at 500 it would be unreachable, since rule 100 already matched and evaluation terminates.

  2. Step 3 is the reason security groups win. The app tier scaled tenfold this morning and no rule changed, because the rule names a group rather than a range. An equivalent NACL rule would have needed a CIDR that either over-permits the whole subnet or goes stale on every scaling event.

  3. Step 5 consulted nothing. The reply was permitted by the tracking entry created in step 4, with no rule evaluation at all. That is what statefulness buys, and it is why the database security group needs no egress rule for replies.

  4. Step 6 is where the classic outage lives. The security group returns ACCEPT and the NACL returns REJECT, so flow logs show two entries for one flow with different verdicts — the signature that distinguishes a NACL problem from a security group problem in about thirty seconds.

  5. The whole trace crossed two NACLs and four security group evaluations. Both layers are always in the path; the design choice is not whether to use NACLs but whether to put policy in them, and here the answer is one deny rule and one ephemeral-range companion, nothing more.

10. When TO Use This

  • Security groups for all service-to-service policy, referencing other groups rather than CIDRs. It is the only formulation that stays correct as workloads scale, and it reads as intent rather than as addresses.

  • A base security group plus service-specific groups. Because attached groups union, composition is safe — adding a group can only widen access, never silently narrow it.

  • NACLs for coarse, documented subnet-wide denies. Incident response against a hostile range, or a guarantee that must hold regardless of what security groups teams attach.

  • Explicit egress rules on security groups when you want outbound control. The default allows all outbound; narrowing it is a real control, and it is the security group half of the egress-filtering story (Item 136).

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Do not put routine policy in NACLs. Statelessness forces wide ephemeral ranges, ordering causes shadowing, and the resulting rule set is harder to read and less restrictive than the security groups it duplicates.

  • Do not expect a NACL to isolate instances within one subnet. NACLs only evaluate traffic crossing the subnet boundary; two instances in the same subnet talk without ever being seen by one.

  • Do not assume security groups reach inside a Kubernetes node. For most CNIs, security groups apply at the node's interface, so pod-to-pod policy needs NetworkPolicy or a mesh's authorization layer as a separate control.

  • Scale limit worth naming: rules per security group and groups per interface are quota-bounded, and the connection tracking table is a finite per-instance resource — an instance with very high connection counts can exhaust it and drop flows that every rule permits.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "NACLs are the stricter layer, so they're the stronger control."

✅ Reality: Statelessness forces you to allow ports 1024–65535 in the return direction, so a NACL that looks locked down is usually admitting a very wide range. Security groups, which need no such allowance, are typically the more restrictive layer in practice.

❌ Misconception: "Security groups have a deny rule for exceptions."

✅ Reality: They are allow-only, and the effective policy is the union of every attached group. There is no way to express "allow this range except that address" — that requires a NACL, and it is the single reason NACLs still exist.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "Changing a security group rule only affects new connections."

✅ Reality: Because the implementation tracks connections, removing an allow rule terminates the flows that rule permitted rather than grandfathering them. Tightening a rule during business hours is therefore an immediate, live change — which is good for incident response and surprising during a routine cleanup.

13. Tech Discussion Traps

Answering "stateful versus stateless" and stopping. It is the memorised line and it survives one follow-up. The version that holds names the consequence: statelessness means the return traffic is a separate decision on an unpredictable ephemeral port, which is why every NACL allow needs a companion rule and why NACL rule sets end up permissive.

Missing the security-group-as-source capability. It is the most operationally significant difference between the two and the one juniors never mention, because it does not appear in the stateful/stateless framing at all. Raising it unprompted reframes the whole comparison around dynamic membership.

Forgetting that NACLs do not see intra-subnet traffic. A design that puts two workloads in one subnet and separates them with a NACL does not work, and the reviewer asking about it is checking exactly this.

Stopping at the network layer for container workloads. Security groups apply at the node interface for most CNIs, so pod-to-pod isolation is not covered by anything discussed here. An answer that presents security groups as complete multi-tenancy isolation on Kubernetes has a gap.

14. Key Numbers & Benchmarks

Metric Value Context Source
Default security group (custom VPC) Deny all inbound, allow all outbound The safe default; outbound is wide open unless narrowed AWS: Security groups
Default NACL (custom VPC) Allow all, both directions A newly created custom NACL is the opposite — deny all AWS: Network ACLs
NACL evaluation Rule-number order, first match wins Unlike security groups, which union all rules AWS: Network ACLs
Ephemeral port range to allow on NACLs 1024–65535 Linux clients default to 32768–60999; the wider range is conventional AWS: Network ACLs
Connection tracking Per-ENI flow table, finite Some all-traffic-allowed flows are untracked to save capacity AWS: EC2 security group connection tracking
NACL scope Subnet boundary only Intra-subnet traffic is never evaluated AWS: Network ACLs

15. Trade-offs & Performance Considerations

Dimension Trade-off
⏱️ Latency Neither layer is a measurable latency cost; NACL rules are evaluated per packet, so very large lists are the only concern
💰 Cost Both are free. The cost of getting them wrong is an outage or an exposure, not a bill
🔒 Security / visibility Security groups express identity-like intent and read well in an audit; NACL rule sets obscure intent behind numbering and ephemeral ranges
📈 Scale The referencing design multiplies rules toward quota; connection tracking is a finite per-instance table
🔧 Ops complexity Two layers with opposite evaluation models is genuinely confusing — which is the argument for keeping policy in one of them
🐛 Debuggability Flow logs record both decisions separately, so an ACCEPT plus a failure is a precise pointer to the other layer

16. Real World Usage

Security-group-references-security-group is the pattern that defines AWS network policy in practice. It survives autoscaling, blue-green deploys and pod churn without a rule change, and it is why mature AWS estates contain very few CIDR-based rules outside the edge.

NACLs are most often used exactly once: during an incident. Blocking a hostile range at the subnet boundary is fast, coarse and effective, and it is the use case that justifies keeping the layer available and otherwise permissive. Estates that put standing policy in NACLs tend to have inherited it from an on-premises firewall model.

Azure merges the two levels into one NSG construct. An Azure NSG is stateful, supports both allow and deny with priority ordering, and can be attached to either a NIC or a subnet — which removes the stateless-return-rule problem entirely while keeping deny. Naming that difference is a useful way to show the AWS split is a design choice rather than a law of cloud networking.

17. Acronym Decoder

  • NACL — Network Access Control List. Each word carries a fact: Network (it sits at the subnet, not the workload), Access Control (allow and deny, unlike a security group), List (ordered and numbered, first match wins).

  • ENI — Elastic Network Interface: the virtual NIC a security group actually attaches to. Worth decoding because it explains why a security group follows an instance rather than an address.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)

  • 122-vpc-mental-model.md — the boundary these controls operate inside

  • 123-subnets-azs-cidr-planning.md — the subnet, which is the NACL's unit of attachment

  • 03-tcp-udp/28-sockets-ports-ephemeral-range.md — the ephemeral range that statelessness forces you to open

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

  • 136-network-security-posture.md — egress filtering, zero-trust and where these controls stop

  • 129-privatelink-vpc-endpoints.md — endpoint policies, a third policy surface at the same boundary

  • Section 13 Kubernetes networking — NetworkPolicy, which covers the pod-to-pod gap

🔀 Alternatives / Competing approaches

  • Kubernetes NetworkPolicy — pod-level policy where security groups stop

  • Service mesh authorization policy — L7 identity-based rules rather than L3/L4 (Section 11, Item 118)

  • AWS Network Firewall — a stateful inspection appliance for the cases both layers here are too coarse for

🧩 Composes with (used together in real systems)

  • VPC flow logs — the only place both decisions become visible

  • Route tables — reachability must exist before policy is consulted at all (Item 125)

  • VPC endpoint policies — resource-level restriction on the endpoint path (Item 129)

19. System Design Application

Skipped — these are policy primitives applied throughout a topology rather than a placeable component; the architect-level treatment is discharged by the Section 3 Tier 4 follow-up, and the system-level posture story belongs to 136-network-security-posture.md.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Peering semantics, non-transitivity and CIDR rules — AWS: How VPC peering connections work

  • Where peering stops scaling — AWS: VPC peering (multi-VPC infrastructure whitepaper)

  • Connection quotas per account — AWS: VPC peering connection quotas

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What does non-transitive mean here? A↔B and B↔C does not give A↔C. Every pair needs its own connection and its own routes.
What blocks a peering outright? Overlapping CIDRs. There is no NAT option — the connection simply cannot be created.
How many connections for a full mesh of n VPCs? n(n−1)/2. Ten VPCs is 45 connections and 90 route table edits.
What must you configure besides the connection? Routes on both sides, and security groups. Accepting the request alone moves no traffic.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

VPC peering is a direct, private L3 link between exactly two VPCs. Traffic uses the AWS backbone rather than the internet, there is no bandwidth bottleneck and no appliance in the path, and within a region it costs nothing extra. Two properties define how it is used: it is non-transitive, so a mesh of n VPCs needs n(n−1)/2 connections and twice that many route entries, and it refuses overlapping CIDRs outright, with no NAT escape hatch. Those two together are why peering is right for a handful of VPCs and why Transit Gateway exists beyond that.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

Why is peering non-transitive, and what does that force you to configure?

Because a peering connection creates a route target, not a forwarding domain. Route tables in VPC A can point A's traffic at the pcx- connection to B, and B's route tables can point at its connection to C — but a packet arriving in B from A does not get re-forwarded onward, because the VPC router will not route between two peering connections. It is a point-to-point link between two address spaces, deliberately.

The practical consequence is that establishing connectivity is a three-part job, and only the first part is the peering connection itself. You must also add routes on both sides — an entry in A's route tables for B's CIDR and vice versa, on every relevant subnet's table — and then allow the traffic in security groups. Forgetting the return route is the most common "the peering is active but nothing works" cause, and it is invisible in the peering connection's own status, which happily reads active.

One useful nuance: within the same region, a security group in one VPC can reference a security group in the peered VPC, so you keep the identity-based policy model across the boundary. That does not work cross-region, where you fall back to CIDR-based rules.

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

Peering or Transit Gateway?

🎯 Really testing: whether you can name the crossover point and price both sides, rather than declaring one modern and one legacy.

Peering wins on cost and latency at small scale. Within a region there is no hourly charge and no per-GB processing charge for the peering itself — you pay only the usual cross-AZ data transfer if the traffic crosses zones — and there is no appliance in the path, so it is as fast as intra-VPC traffic. For two or three VPCs that need to talk, it is strictly simpler than anything else.

Transit Gateway wins on manageability the moment the count grows. It is a hub: each VPC attaches once, routing is centralised in the gateway's own route tables, and adding the eleventh VPC is one attachment rather than ten new peerings and twenty route edits. It is also transitive by design and supports segmentation through multiple gateway route tables. The costs are real and per-unit: an hourly charge per attachment plus a per-GB data processing charge on everything that crosses it — so at high traffic volumes between two specific VPCs, a direct peering alongside the gateway is a legitimate optimisation.

My crossover is around four to five VPCs, or sooner if the connectivity requirement is "everything talks to everything". Below that, peering is less machinery and less money. Above it, n(n−1)/2 route management becomes the failure mode: not because it cannot be expressed in Terraform, but because nobody can reason about which paths exist, and the route tables drift.

4. Quick Comparison Table

VPC peering Transit Gateway
Topology Point-to-point, non-transitive Hub-and-spoke, transitive
Connections for n VPCs n(n−1)/2 n attachments
Cost (same region) No hourly, no per-GB for the link Hourly per attachment + per GB processed
Latency No appliance in the path One hop through the gateway
Overlapping CIDRs Refused Refused
Cross-VPC security group references Yes, same region only No
Segmentation Implicit — a link exists or it does not Explicit, via multiple gateway route tables
When you'd actually pick it Two to four VPCs, or a high-volume pair alongside a hub Five or more, or anything needing central policy

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The mesh arithmetic is the whole scaling story. A full mesh of n VPCs needs n(n−1)/2 peering connections: 3 VPCs is 3 connections, 5 is 10, 10 is 45, and 20 is 190. Each connection needs a route entry in every relevant route table on both sides, so the route-edit count is roughly 2 × connections × route-tables-per-VPC — for ten VPCs with three route tables each, that is on the order of 270 entries to create and keep correct. Peering connection quotas per VPC and per account are finite too, and the mesh reaches them well before the operational burden becomes bearable.

The CIDR constraint is binary and permanent. Two VPCs with any overlap cannot be peered, and unlike some routing problems there is no partial mitigation — the route table cannot express two destinations for one prefix, so AWS refuses the connection rather than creating something ambiguous. This is why the address plan in Item 123 matters: it is not tidiness, it is the thing that keeps peering available as an option for connections you have not designed yet.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Do not build a mesh beyond a handful of VPCs. n(n−1)/2 connections and hundreds of route entries stop being reviewable long before they stop being expressible, and drift between the two sides of a pair is silent.

  • Do not expect peering to solve overlapping CIDRs. It refuses them outright. The only workarounds are renumbering one side or NAT-ing between them through an appliance, both of which are worse than having planned addresses.

  • Do not assume accepting the peering request establishes connectivity. Routes on both sides and security group rules are separate steps; the connection reads active while carrying no traffic at all.

  • Do not use peering to reach a shared service that many VPCs need. That is a hub or a PrivateLink endpoint service pattern; peering every consumer to the provider VPC recreates the mesh problem with extra exposure, since a peering grants routing to the whole CIDR rather than to one service.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "Peering has a bandwidth or throughput bottleneck."

✅ Reality: There is no appliance in the path and no aggregate bandwidth limit imposed by the peering itself — traffic crosses the AWS backbone at instance-level speeds. The reasons to move to a Transit Gateway are topology management and central policy, not throughput.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "Peering VPC A to B gives A access to everything B can reach."

✅ Reality: Non-transitivity means A reaches B's own CIDR and nothing beyond it — not B's other peers, not B's NAT gateway, not B's VPC endpoints. Every one of those is a separate design decision, and expecting transitive reachability is the most common misunderstanding of what a peering actually grants.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

  • 125-route-tables.md — the two-sided route entries that make a peering carry traffic

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

notes.title: Transit Gateway & Hub-and-Spoke

headings.text: Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)
How does segmentation actually work in a Transit Gateway?
Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)
Is centralised egress through a Transit Gateway worth it?
⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)
⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • What a Transit Gateway is and how attachments route — AWS: What is AWS Transit Gateway for Amazon VPC?

  • Where it sits among the connectivity options — AWS: AWS Transit Gateway (VPC connectivity options whitepaper)

  • Centralised egress and shared-service patterns behind a hub — AWS: Using NAT Gateways with multiple Amazon VPCs at scale

  • Bonus — AWS: Amazon VPC Pricing

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What does it change versus peering? Transitive routing through a hub: n attachments instead of n(n−1)/2 connections.
How is segmentation expressed? Multiple TGW route tables — an attachment associates with one, and propagates into others.
What does it charge? Hourly per attachment plus per GB processed — every crossing is metered.
Does it fix overlapping CIDRs? No. Same constraint as peering; the address plan still has to be right.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

A Transit Gateway is a regional routing hub. Each VPC, VPN or Direct Connect gateway attaches once, and the hub's own route tables decide which attachments can reach which — so connectivity becomes n attachments rather than a mesh of n(n−1)/2 peerings, and it is transitive by design. Segmentation is expressed by giving the hub several route tables: production attachments associate with one, non-production with another, and a shared-services VPC propagates into both. The cost is that it is metered per attachment-hour and per gigabyte processed, so every crossing has a price that a peering did not.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

How does segmentation actually work in a Transit Gateway?

Through two separate operations that people conflate. An attachment associates with exactly one TGW route table — that is the table consulted when traffic arrives from that attachment, and it determines where that VPC may send traffic. An attachment propagates its routes into zero or more TGW route tables — that is how other attachments learn how to reach it.

Those two knobs give you segmentation without any firewall. To isolate production from staging: create two route tables, associate production attachments with the production table and staging attachments with the staging table, and propagate each environment's routes only into its own table. Neither can route to the other because neither's associated table contains the other's prefixes. To add a shared-services VPC reachable by both, propagate its routes into both tables while associating it with a table that contains both environments — a common and deliberately asymmetric arrangement.

The reason this matters is that it moves segmentation from n VPC route tables into a handful of hub tables. In a peering mesh, "staging must not reach production" is enforced by the absence of routes in many places, which is unauditable; here it is two tables you can read.

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

Is centralised egress through a Transit Gateway worth it?

📍 Seen in the wild: the follow-up once a hub is on the diagram and someone notices every VPC still has its own NAT gateways.

🎯 Really testing: whether you can do the arithmetic rather than assuming centralisation is automatically better.

The case for centralising is that NAT gateways per AZ per VPC multiply fast — twenty VPCs across three AZs is sixty gateways and sixty hourly charges — and that egress policy, inspection and audit want one home rather than twenty. Collapsing to one egress VPC with three NAT gateways behind the hub removes fifty-seven hourly charges and gives you a single place to put a forward proxy or a firewall.

The case against is that every byte now pays Transit Gateway data processing on top of NAT processing and internet egress, where before it paid only the latter two. So the trade is fixed hourly charges (which centralisation removes) against a per-gigabyte charge (which centralisation adds), and the crossover depends entirely on traffic volume per VPC. A large number of low-traffic VPCs centralises well; a small number of very high-egress VPCs does not, and the honest answer for those is to keep local NAT gateways even inside a hub topology.

The tiebreaker is usually not cost. If you need hostname-level egress control and per-tenant audit — which any AI platform running agent tool-calling does — then the inspection tier has to exist somewhere, and having twenty copies of it is worse than paying the hub's per-GB charge for one. I would centralise for the policy and then exempt the two or three highest-volume VPCs with local egress, rather than treating it as all-or-nothing.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Peering mesh Transit Gateway Cloud WAN / multi-region hub
Links for n VPCs n(n−1)/2 n attachments n per region, regions interconnected
Transitive No Yes Yes
Segmentation Absence of routes, scattered Hub route tables, auditable Policy-defined segments
Cost shape Free link, cross-AZ transfer only Hourly per attachment + per GB Higher fixed, similar per GB
Latency No appliance hop One hub hop One or more hub hops
Best at 2–4 VPCs, or a high-volume pair 5+ VPCs in a region Many regions, policy-driven segments

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The link arithmetic is the reason the hub exists. Peering needs n(n−1)/2 connections; a hub needs n. At ten VPCs that is 45 versus 10, and at twenty it is 190 versus 20 — and the route-entry count scales with the connection count, so the operational burden diverges even faster than the link count.

The cost arithmetic runs the other way. Every attachment carries an hourly charge, and every gigabyte crossing the gateway carries a data processing charge — including traffic that would have been free over a same-region peering. So a hub converts a topology problem into a per-GB line item, which is the right trade when connectivity is broad and low-volume, and the wrong one for two chatty VPCs that could simply be peered directly. Running a direct peering alongside the hub for such a pair is a legitimate and common optimisation, not a hack.

Attachments are AZ-aware. A TGW attachment is created in specific subnets, one per AZ, and traffic entering the gateway from an AZ that has no attachment subnet must first cross to one that does — incurring cross-AZ transfer. Creating attachment subnets in every AZ the VPC uses is a small detail with a recurring per-GB cost attached to getting it wrong.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Do not adopt a hub for two or three VPCs. Peering is free within a region and has no appliance hop; a Transit Gateway there is per-GB charges and an extra component for connectivity you already had.

  • Do not route very high-volume, VPC-to-VPC traffic through the hub if a direct peering will do. Data processing charges on a multi-terabyte flow dwarf the hourly savings; peer the pair and keep the hub for everything else.

  • Do not assume the hub gives you inspection. It routes; it does not filter. Firewalls, proxies and inspection appliances are separate attachments that traffic must be routed through, which is a deliberate route table design rather than a property of the gateway.

  • Do not expect it to resolve CIDR overlaps. The same constraint as peering applies, and a hub makes it worse in one respect: a single overlap can block an attachment that many VPCs depend on.

  • Do not forget attachment subnets in every AZ in use. A missing attachment subnet silently adds a cross-AZ hop and a per-GB charge to every flow from that zone.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "Transit Gateway replaces peering."

✅ Reality: They coexist deliberately. The hub handles broad, low-to-moderate-volume connectivity and policy; direct peerings remain the right answer for high-volume pairs, because a same-region peering has no per-GB processing charge at all. Mature topologies run both.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "Attaching a VPC to the Transit Gateway connects it to everything else attached."

✅ Reality: An attachment only reaches what its associated TGW route table contains, and it is only reachable by tables it propagates into. Association and propagation are two independent operations, and a VPC attached with neither configured correctly is connected to precisely nothing — which is also how segmentation is enforced.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

headings.text: Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)
How does an interface endpoint actually intercept traffic to a public service name?
Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)
Interface endpoints in every VPC, or a centralised endpoint VPC?
⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)
⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Gateway endpoints — the free, route-table kind — AWS: Gateway endpoints

  • PrivateLink as an architecture, including endpoint services — AWS: AWS PrivateLink (multi-VPC infrastructure whitepaper)

  • Centralising interface endpoints across many VPCs — AWS: Centralized access to VPC private endpoints

  • Bonus — AWS: Amazon VPC Pricing

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Gateway vs interface endpoint — the mechanism? Gateway: a prefix-list route. Interface: an ENI with a private IP and private DNS.
Which is free? Gateway endpoints (S3, DynamoDB only). Interface endpoints charge hourly per AZ plus per GB.
What does an endpoint give you over NAT? Traffic never leaves the AWS network, no NAT processing charge, and a resource-level endpoint policy.
What does PrivateLink expose, versus peering? One service behind an NLB — not a whole CIDR. Consumers get no routing into your VPC.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

VPC endpoints let workloads reach managed services without traversing the internet or a NAT gateway. There are two mechanisms. A gateway endpoint — S3 and DynamoDB only — adds a prefix-list entry to your route tables, is free, and removes NAT processing charges outright. An interface endpoint creates an ENI with a private address in your subnets and overrides the service's DNS name to resolve there, costing hourly per AZ plus per gigabyte. The same interface mechanism, exposed by you rather than by AWS, is PrivateLink: you publish one service behind a Network Load Balancer, and consumers reach exactly that service with no routing into your VPC at all.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

How does an interface endpoint actually intercept traffic to a public service name?

Through DNS, not routing. Creating an interface endpoint with private DNS enabled causes the service's public hostname — secretsmanager.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com, say — to resolve inside your VPC to the endpoint ENI's private address instead of a public one. The application does not change, the SDK does not change, and the code still uses the public endpoint name; only the answer to the DNS query changes.

That has two implications worth stating. First, enable_dns_support and enable_dns_hostnames must be on or the interception silently does not happen and traffic goes out through NAT as before, costing money while appearing to work. Second, the endpoint is an ENI in a specific subnet in a specific AZ, so you create one per AZ for availability, and each one is a billable resource — which is why the hourly cost of interface endpoints scales with AZ count and service count.

A gateway endpoint works by the opposite mechanism: no ENI, no DNS change, just a route table entry pointing an AWS-managed prefix list at the endpoint. That is why it is free — there is no resource to run — and also why it only exists for S3 and DynamoDB and only works from within the VPC that holds the route table.

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

Interface endpoints in every VPC, or a centralised endpoint VPC?

🎯 Really testing: whether you notice that the per-AZ, per-service hourly charge multiplies across a large estate.

Endpoints in every VPC are simplest and have no extra hop. The problem is multiplication: the hourly charge is per endpoint per AZ, so twenty VPCs × three AZs × eight services is 480 billable endpoint-AZs, which becomes a serious line item for what is essentially plumbing.

Centralising puts the interface endpoints in one shared-services VPC behind a Transit Gateway, with private hosted zones shared to the consumer VPCs so DNS still resolves to them. That collapses 480 down to 24. The costs are a Transit Gateway data processing charge on traffic that previously stayed local, a more complex DNS arrangement (you now manage the hosted zone associations yourself, because cross-VPC private DNS does not happen automatically), and a shared failure domain for every service call in the estate.

My rule: gateway endpoints everywhere always, because they are free and there is no argument against them. Interface endpoints locally while the VPC count is small, and centralised once the endpoint-AZ count runs into the hundreds — at which point the per-GB hub charge is comfortably less than the hourly sprawl. And regardless of the choice, put the highest-traffic services' endpoints local, since those are the ones where per-GB charges dominate.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Gateway endpoint Interface endpoint (PrivateLink) PrivateLink endpoint service (yours) VPC peering
Mechanism Route table prefix list ENI + private DNS override ENI → your NLB Route table → pcx
Services S3, DynamoDB only Most AWS services, SaaS partners Anything you put behind an NLB Whole VPC CIDR
Cost Free Hourly per AZ + per GB Hourly per AZ + per GB Free in-region
Exposure granted The service only The service only One service, one port The entire peered CIDR
Direction Consumer → service Consumer → service Consumer → provider, one-way Bidirectional
Overlapping CIDRs Irrelevant Irrelevant Works anyway Refused
When you'd actually pick it Always, for S3 and DynamoDB Keeping AWS-service traffic off NAT Exposing a service to customers or other teams Broad connectivity between your own VPCs

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The saving is two charges, not one. Traffic to an AWS service through NAT pays NAT data processing and internet egress; through an endpoint it pays neither for a gateway endpoint, and only the endpoint's own per-GB charge for an interface endpoint. For S3 at terabyte scale the gateway endpoint is a pure, free elimination of both — which is why it is the most reliably recommended cost fix in AWS.

The endpoint policy is a distinct control surface. An endpoint carries its own IAM-style resource policy that constrains what can be reached through it — for example, restricting an S3 gateway endpoint to your own buckets only. That is a genuine data-exfiltration control that neither security groups nor NACLs can express, because it operates on resources rather than addresses, and it is the strongest security argument for endpoints over NAT.

PrivateLink inverts the exposure model. A peering grants routing to an entire CIDR in both directions; a PrivateLink endpoint service grants a consumer access to exactly one NLB on one port, one-way, with no route into your VPC and no CIDR coordination — so it works even when both sides use 10.0.0.0/16. That last property makes it the standard mechanism for exposing a service to customers or to teams whose address plans you do not control.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Do not skip gateway endpoints. They are free, take one route table entry, and remove NAT processing on what is often the largest flow in the account. There is no scenario where omitting one is correct.

  • Do not create interface endpoints for every service in every VPC reflexively. The hourly charge is per endpoint per AZ and multiplies fast; audit which services actually carry meaningful traffic before blanketing the estate.

  • Do not enable an interface endpoint with VPC DNS support disabled. Private DNS is the interception mechanism; without it the endpoint exists, bills you, and intercepts nothing while traffic continues out through NAT.

  • Do not use peering where PrivateLink fits. Exposing one service does not require granting routing to a whole CIDR, and a peering additionally forces CIDR coordination you may not control.

  • Scale limit worth naming: interface endpoints are ENIs, so they consume subnet addresses and are bound to an AZ — endpoint sprawl is both a cost and an address-plan consumer.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "All VPC endpoints are basically the same thing."

✅ Reality: Gateway endpoints are a free route table entry for two services; interface endpoints are billable ENIs with DNS interception for many. They differ in mechanism, cost, coverage and failure mode, and conflating them leads to either paying for something free or expecting free something that is not.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "Traffic to S3 from a private subnet stays inside AWS anyway, so an endpoint is only a security nicety."

✅ Reality: S3 resolves to public addresses, so without a gateway endpoint that traffic takes the full NAT path and is charged NAT processing per gigabyte. The endpoint is a cost fix first and a security control second — and at multi-terabyte volumes it is the single largest avoidable line item in a typical account.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

  • 125-route-tables.md — prefix-list routing, which is how gateway endpoints work

  • 133-private-dns-cloud.md — the DNS interception interface endpoints depend on

  • 136-network-security-posture.md — endpoint policies as an exfiltration control

  • 128-transit-gateway.md — the hub that makes centralised endpoints workable

notes.title: Site-to-Site VPN vs Direct Connect

headings.text: 📚 Reference Links
1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)
2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The VPN option — AWS: What is AWS Site-to-Site VPN?

  • Combining both for resilience — AWS: AWS Direct Connect + AWS Site-to-Site VPN

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The core difference? VPN runs encrypted over the public internet; Direct Connect is a dedicated private circuit.
Why is VPN latency variable? It traverses the internet, so jitter and path changes are inherited. Direct Connect is a fixed path.
What is the usual production pattern? Direct Connect as primary, VPN as encrypted backup over a different path.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Both connect an on-premises network to a cloud VPC, and they trade the same three things in opposite directions. Site-to-site VPN is IPsec over the public internet: available in minutes, cheap, encrypted by construction, and subject to internet latency, jitter and bandwidth variability. Direct Connect — with ExpressRoute and Cloud Interconnect as the Azure and GCP equivalents — is a dedicated physical circuit into a provider facility: consistent latency, committed bandwidth, lower per-GB egress rates at volume, and a lead time measured in weeks plus a cross-connect fee. Direct Connect is not encrypted by default, so regulated workloads run IPsec or MACsec over it. The standard production shape is Direct Connect as primary with a VPN standing by as failover, because the two fail for independent reasons.

notes.title: Client VPN, Bastion & SSM Patterns for Operator Access

headings.text: 📚 Reference Links
1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)
2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The no-inbound-port approach — AWS: AWS Systems Manager Session Manager

  • Bonus — AWS: Security best practices for Systems Manager

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What makes Session Manager different from a bastion? No inbound port, no public IP, no SSH keys — the agent dials out to the service.
What does it use for authorisation and audit? IAM for access, CloudTrail plus session logs for audit. Not SSH keys.
When is a client VPN still the right answer? When operators need general network access, not just a shell on specific instances.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Three ways to give an engineer access to a private network, in increasing order of preference. A bastion host is a hardened instance with a public IP that you SSH through — it works, and it means an inbound port on the internet, key distribution, and a host to patch. A client VPN puts the operator's laptop on the network, which is right when they need broad access to many resources, and carries the usual credential and split-tunnel questions. Session Manager inverts the model entirely: an agent on the instance dials out to the service, so there is no inbound port, no public IP and no SSH key anywhere; access is granted by IAM policy and every session is logged to CloudTrail and optionally recorded. That combination — no listening port plus identity-based authorisation plus a complete audit trail — is why it has largely displaced bastions for shell access, with client VPN reserved for cases needing genuine network reachability rather than a terminal.

notes.title: Load Balancer Types in Cloud

headings.text: Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)
What forces the choice, other than the layer?
Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)
NLB in front of an ingress controller, or ALB straight to services?
⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)
⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The L7 option and its features — AWS: Application Load Balancers

  • The L4 option, static IPs and flow timeouts — AWS: Network Load Balancers

  • The Azure equivalents, and why there are two — Microsoft Learn: What is Azure Application Gateway

  • Bonus — Microsoft Learn: Azure Networking Services and Categories

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
ALB vs NLB in one line? ALB is L7 (HTTP, per-request, path routing); NLB is L4 (TCP/UDP, per-connection, static IP).
Which gives a static IP? NLB — and it can hold an Elastic IP. ALB is a DNS name whose addresses rotate.
Which preserves the client source IP by default? NLB. ALB puts it in X-Forwarded-For and the socket shows the balancer.
Why is CLB deprecated in practice? It predates the L4/L7 split, does both badly, and has no feature parity with either.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

AWS splits its balancers by layer. An ALB is L7: it terminates TLS, routes on host and path, balances per request, retries, and integrates with WAF and OIDC. An NLB is L4: it forwards TCP and UDP flows, preserves the client source IP, holds a static or Elastic IP, and scales to very high throughput with almost no added latency. The Classic Load Balancer predates the split and does neither well — treat it as legacy. GCP and Azure make the same cut with different names: Application Load Balancer and Application Gateway at L7, Network Load Balancer and Azure Load Balancer at L4.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

What forces the choice, other than the layer?

Three managed-service specifics decide it more often than the L4/L7 theory does. Addressing: an ALB is a DNS name whose underlying addresses change, so a client that can only be configured with an IP — an appliance, a partner's firewall allow-list — needs an NLB, which supports a static Elastic IP per AZ. Source IP: an NLB delivers the client's real address to the target, while an ALB terminates and moves it into X-Forwarded-For, so anything doing IP-based logic without header trust needs the NLB.

Protocol is the third. An ALB speaks HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and gRPC and nothing else; anything that is not HTTP-shaped — a database protocol, a broker, UDP — must use an NLB, and the L7 feature set is unavailable by construction. That is why a design serving both HTTP and a non-HTTP protocol ends up with two balancers rather than one, and it is a perfectly ordinary outcome rather than a failure of consolidation.

The layer-level trade-offs behind all this — per-request versus per-connection balancing, retries, deep health checks — are Section 11's Item 108; this note is about which product expresses them.

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

NLB in front of an ingress controller, or ALB straight to services?

🎯 Really testing: whether you notice the duplication when two L7 tiers stack.

An ALB straight to Kubernetes services (via the load balancer controller) gives managed L7 with WAF and OIDC and no cluster component to operate, at the cost of provisioning an AWS resource per Ingress unless you consolidate, and of routing rules living in AWS rather than in the cluster's own API.

An NLB in front of an in-cluster ingress controller keeps all L7 behaviour in one place — the controller — and gets packets in cheaply with the source IP preserved. That matters for HTTP/2 and gRPC especially: the ingress controller can balance per request across pods, which an L4 hop alone cannot (Section 11, Item 114). The cost is that you now operate the controller, and WAF integration becomes your problem rather than a checkbox.

My rule: if the cluster already runs a well-operated ingress controller or a mesh gateway, NLB plus that controller is less duplication and better gRPC behaviour. If there is no platform team and the requirement is "expose this service safely", the ALB path is the honest answer. The wrong shape is an ALB in front of an ingress controller, which terminates TLS twice, routes twice, and gives you two places to configure timeouts for no gain.

4. Quick Comparison Table

ALB (L7) NLB (L4) GCP Azure
Layer HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, gRPC TCP, UDP, TLS pass-through Application LB / Network LB Application Gateway / Load Balancer
Balancing unit Per request Per connection Same split Same split
Static IP No — DNS name only Yes, Elastic IP per AZ Global anycast IP at L7 Yes
Client source IP at target In X-Forwarded-For Preserved Header at L7, preserved at L4 Header at L7, preserved at L4
TLS termination Yes Optional Yes Yes
WAF / auth integration Native None Cloud Armor WAF on App Gateway
Idle timeout 60 s default, configurable 350 s default, configurable 60–6000 s Configurable Configurable
When you'd actually pick it HTTP services needing routing, WAF, auth Static IP, non-HTTP protocols, extreme throughput, in front of a mesh gateway — —

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The two timeout defaults are the ones that bite. An ALB's idle timeout defaults to 60 seconds — raise it for streaming or long-poll routes or connections get cut mid-response. An NLB's TCP idle timeout defaults to 350 seconds and is configurable from 60 to 6000, so a connection pool idle for six minutes comes back dead unless you raise it or send keepalives below it; the failure looks like the database rather than the balancer, because the client only learns on the next write, when it receives a RST.

Raising the NLB timeout has a second half people miss. Above 350 seconds you must also raise the target instance's ENI connection-tracking idle timeout (TcpEstablishedTimeout), which defaults to 350 seconds on current Nitro generations. Leaving them mismatched means the instance stops tracking the flow while the balancer still considers it live, and the result is dropped packets on a connection both ends believe is healthy.

Both scale by adding capacity you do not see, and both consume subnet addresses to do it. Each balancer places interfaces in the subnets you nominate, so a subnet too small to grow them constrains the balancer — a real and easily-missed consequence of the sizing decisions in Item 123. AWS guidance is to leave several free addresses per AZ per balancer for scaling headroom.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Do not put an ALB in front of an ingress controller. Two L7 tiers means two TLS terminations, two routing rule sets and two timeout hierarchies for one request path, with no capability gained.

  • Do not use an NLB for HTTP/2 or gRPC to a pod fleet without an L7 hop behind it. Per-connection balancing pins every request on a connection to one backend (Section 11, Item 114).

  • Do not leave the NLB idle timeout at its 350-second default for pooled or long-lived connections. Either raise it — remembering to raise the target ENI's TcpEstablishedTimeout to match — or configure client-side keepalives below it. Doing neither is the most common source of "the first query after a quiet period always fails".

  • Do not choose the Classic Load Balancer for anything new. It predates the layer split, lacks the feature set of both successors, and exists only for workloads that have not migrated.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "ALB and NLB are the same product at different price points."

✅ Reality: They operate at different layers and therefore have disjoint capability sets. An NLB cannot route by path or retry a request; an ALB cannot give you a static IP, preserve the source IP on the socket, or carry a non-HTTP protocol. Neither is a cheaper version of the other.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "Raising the NLB idle timeout is a one-line fix for dropped pooled connections."

✅ Reality: It is one line at the balancer and a second, easily forgotten one at the target. Above 350 seconds the instance's ENI connection-tracking timeout (TcpEstablishedTimeout, also 350 s by default on current Nitro generations) must be raised to match, or the instance stops tracking a flow the balancer still considers live and packets are dropped on a connection both ends believe is healthy.
