  • Bonus — AWS: Understanding Amazon DNS

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Where does a VPC's resolver live? VPC CIDR base + 2 — 10.20.0.2 for 10.20.0.0/16. Also reachable at 169.254.169.253.
What is split-horizon DNS? The same name resolving to a private address inside the VPC and a public one outside.
Inbound vs outbound resolver endpoint? Inbound: on-prem queries AWS. Outbound: AWS queries on-prem, via forwarding rules.
Which VPC setting breaks everything here? enableDnsSupport off — no resolver, so private zones and interface endpoints stop working.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Every VPC has a resolver at its CIDR base plus two, and it answers three kinds of query: names in private hosted zones associated with that VPC, AWS service names — including the interface endpoints that override them — and everything else recursively. A private hosted zone is a normal DNS zone visible only to the VPCs you associate it with, which is what makes split-horizon possible: api.example.com resolving to a private address inside and a public one on the internet. Resolver endpoints extend this across the boundary, inbound so on-premises can query AWS names and outbound so AWS can forward to corporate DNS.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

What decides which answer a VPC resolver gives?

Specificity of the zone, evaluated much like routing. If a private hosted zone associated with the VPC covers the queried name, that zone answers and the query never goes public. If an interface endpoint has private DNS enabled for an AWS service name, that override answers. Otherwise the resolver recurses to the public DNS.

The consequence people trip over is that private hosted zones are matched on the most specific zone, and a matching zone answers authoritatively even for names it does not contain. If you associate a private zone for example.com with a VPC and it holds only api.example.com, then a query for www.example.com returns NXDOMAIN from that zone rather than falling through to the public example.com — because the private zone owns the namespace. That single behaviour is behind most "it resolves everywhere except in the VPC" incidents, and the fix is to hold the full record set in the private zone or to scope the zone more narrowly.

The association model is the other half. A private hosted zone is visible to exactly the VPCs associated with it, and cross-account association is an explicit two-step authorisation. So a shared services zone must be associated with every consumer VPC — it is not inherited through peering or a Transit Gateway, which surprises people who assume connectivity implies name resolution.

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

How should a multi-VPC estate resolve shared service names?

🎯 Really testing: whether you separate connectivity from resolution, which are independent problems.

The naive answer is to associate one shared private hosted zone with every VPC. It works, it is simple, and the association count grows linearly with VPCs — but cross-account association requires an authorisation step per VPC, so at scale it becomes a piece of automation nobody owns, and a VPC created without it has connectivity and no names.

The alternative is Route 53 Resolver rules shared through Resource Access Manager: define forwarding rules once in a networking account and share them, so consumer VPCs forward queries for a domain to a central resolver rather than each holding an association. That centralises the change surface and scales better, at the cost of an outbound resolver endpoint and a per-query charge, plus a shared dependency for name resolution across the estate.

My rule is to associate directly while the VPC count is small and the zones are few, and to move to shared resolver rules once either number grows — with the specific trigger being the first time someone creates a VPC that can route to a service but cannot resolve it. That failure is the signal that resolution has stopped tracking connectivity, and it is worth naming because the two are configured in completely different places.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Mechanism Answers for Scope Cost shape When you'd actually pick it
VPC resolver (base + 2) Everything, by default One VPC Free Always present; the entry point
Private hosted zone Names you define VPCs you associate Per zone, per query Internal service names, split-horizon
Interface endpoint private DNS AWS service names The VPC holding the endpoint Part of the endpoint charge Keeping AWS traffic off NAT (Item 129)
Inbound resolver endpoint AWS names, queried from on-prem Region Hourly per ENI + per query Hybrid: on-prem must resolve cloud names
Outbound resolver endpoint + rules On-prem or shared names, queried from AWS Region, shareable Hourly per ENI + per query Hybrid, or centralised multi-VPC resolution

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The resolver has a per-interface query limit. Amazon-provided DNS enforces a packets-per-second cap per network interface toward the .2 resolver, and a workload that resolves aggressively — short DNS caching in a client library, a service mesh resolving on every call, a batch job fanning out — hits it. It presents as intermittent resolution failures under load with no configuration change, and the fixes are client-side caching, a local caching resolver such as NodeLocal DNSCache in Kubernetes, or spreading the load across more interfaces. It is one of the few hard limits in this section that a workload can reach through ordinary behaviour.

Split-horizon works because the private zone is consulted first and authoritatively. That is a feature when you want internal callers to reach an internal address for a public name, and a trap when the private zone is incomplete: the zone owns the whole namespace it covers, so any name it lacks returns NXDOMAIN rather than falling through. Scope private zones as narrowly as the names you actually intend to override.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Do not associate a broad private hosted zone to override one name. The zone becomes authoritative for the entire namespace inside the VPC, so every sibling name it does not contain starts returning NXDOMAIN. Use the narrowest zone that covers the names you are overriding.

  • Do not assume routing implies resolution. A peering or Transit Gateway attachment gives connectivity; private hosted zones must be associated separately with each VPC, and shared resolver rules must be shared separately. The two are configured in different places and drift apart quietly.

  • Do not disable enableDnsSupport on a VPC. It removes the .2 resolver, which silently breaks private zones, interface endpoints and anything relying on DNS-based service discovery.

  • Do not resolve aggressively without caching. The per-interface query limit toward the VPC resolver is reachable by ordinary workloads, and the failure appears as intermittent, load-correlated resolution errors rather than as a rate limit.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "A private hosted zone is private because it holds internal addresses."

✅ Reality: It is private because it is only visible to the VPCs it is associated with. It can hold any records at all, including public addresses, and its privacy is an association property rather than anything about the data in it.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "If a private zone doesn't have the record, the query falls through to public DNS."

✅ Reality: It does not. A matching private hosted zone answers authoritatively for its entire namespace, so a missing record returns NXDOMAIN inside the VPC while the same name resolves fine everywhere else. This asymmetry is the single most confusing behaviour in cloud DNS, and it looks like a broken resolver rather than a zone-scope decision.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

  • 04-dns/34-private-dns-service-discovery.md — private naming as a general pattern

  • 122-vpc-mental-model.md — the .2 resolver and the DNS attributes that enable it

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

  • 129-privatelink-vpc-endpoints.md — interface endpoints work entirely through DNS override

  • 135-multi-region-networking.md — resolution across regions and its failover behaviour

  • 04-dns/32-ttl-and-caching-layers.md — why client-side caching decides whether you hit the query limit

headings.text: Where the meters are
The stacking table — one request, several meters
The fixes, ranked by return
Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)
Why is cross-AZ traffic charged in both directions?
Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)
How far should you go to keep traffic in one AZ?
⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)
⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

notes.html:
📋 Table topic. Per the TABLE / PLAYBOOK rule, Section 4 is the centrepiece and sits above Section 3, and Section 6 is discharged by the arithmetic rather than a mechanism diagram.

📚 Reference Links

  • The authoritative rate card — check it, do not memorise it — AWS: Amazon VPC Pricing

  • Where the charges land in real topologies — AWS: Overview of Data Transfer Costs for Common Architectures

  • The container-specific version, including cross-AZ pod traffic — AWS: Understanding data transfer costs for AWS container services

  • Bonus — AWS: NAT gateways

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Which boundary is free? Same-AZ, same-VPC, private addresses. Cross that AZ line and it is metered.
How many meters can one NAT'd internet request hit? Up to three or four: cross-AZ, NAT processing, internet egress — and TGW processing if hubbed.
Which direction is cross-AZ charged? Both. In and out, per gigabyte, on each side of the flow.
The single highest-return fix? An S3 gateway endpoint — free, one route entry, removes NAT processing entirely.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Cloud networking is nearly free inside one availability zone and metered every time traffic crosses a boundary. The boundaries that cost money are the AZ line, the NAT gateway, the region line, the internet, and any hub the traffic passes through — and they stack, so one request from a private subnet to the internet can be billed three or four times over. Nothing on an architecture diagram shows this, which is why it surprises architects: a design chosen for symmetry across three AZs is also a design that pays per gigabyte for its own internal chatter.

4. Quick Comparison Table — the centrepiece

Where the meters are

Boundary crossed Charged? Direction Typical remedy
Same AZ, same VPC, private IPs Free — The baseline; keep chatty services here
Cross-AZ within a VPC Yes, per GB Both in and out AZ-aware routing; topology-aware hints in Kubernetes
Through a NAT gateway Hourly + per GB processed Processed bytes VPC endpoints; per-AZ gateways to avoid stacking cross-AZ
To the internet Per GB out (in is free) Egress only CDN in front; compression; keep data in-region
Cross-region Per GB, both regions may charge Both Replicate rather than call; region-local reads
Through a Transit Gateway Hourly per attachment + per GB Processed bytes Direct peering for high-volume pairs
VPC peering, same region Free link; cross-AZ still applies — Prefer for chatty pairs over a hub
Gateway endpoint (S3, DynamoDB) Free — Always create them
Interface endpoint Hourly per AZ + per GB Processed bytes Centralise once the endpoint-AZ count is large
Via a CDN CDN egress rates, usually below origin egress Egress Cache aggressively; origin shield

⚠️ Rates change and vary by region. This note deliberately gives the shape of the charges rather than dollar figures; check the pricing page for current rates before quoting a number, and never quote one from memory in a design discussion.

The stacking table — one request, several meters

Scenario Meters hit Avoidable?
App → S3, no gateway endpoint NAT processing + internet egress (+ cross-AZ if the NAT is in another zone) Entirely — free gateway endpoint
App → vendor API via NAT in another AZ Cross-AZ + NAT processing + internet egress Partly — per-AZ NAT removes one meter
Pod → pod across AZs Cross-AZ, both directions Yes — topology-aware routing keeps traffic zonal
App → managed service via interface endpoint Endpoint hourly + endpoint per-GB Cheaper than NAT, not free
Cross-region replication Cross-region egress, possibly both sides Reduce volume; compress; batch
Spoke VPC → internet via hub egress VPC TGW processing + NAT processing + internet egress Local NAT for the highest-volume VPCs

The fixes, ranked by return

  • Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB. Free, one route table entry, removes the largest avoidable line item in most accounts.

  • NAT gateway per AZ. Removes a cross-AZ meter from most egress; the hourly cost is usually less than the transfer it saves.

  • Keep chatty service pairs in one AZ where availability allows, or make the client AZ-aware so it prefers a same-zone endpoint.

  • A CDN in front of anything high-volume and cacheable. CDN egress is typically cheaper than origin egress, and cached bytes cost origin nothing at all.

  • Direct peering alongside a hub for the two or three heaviest VPC pairs. Same-region peering has no per-GB link charge; a Transit Gateway does.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

Why is cross-AZ traffic charged in both directions?

Because each side's transfer is metered independently: the sending instance is charged for data out of its AZ, and the receiving instance is charged for data in to its. So a request-response pair between two AZs is billed on the request in both directions and again on the response — which makes the effective rate for a chatty synchronous workload roughly double what a naive one-way calculation suggests.

It surprises people because the identical traffic inside one AZ is free, so the marginal cost of spreading across zones is a per-gigabyte charge on traffic the application does not know has moved. Kubernetes worsens it by default: a Service balances across all ready pods regardless of zone, so roughly two thirds of pod-to-pod calls in a three-AZ cluster cross a boundary unless topology-aware routing is on.

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

How far should you go to keep traffic in one AZ?

🎯 Really testing: whether you will trade availability for cost, and where you draw the line.

Not far, for anything on the critical path. Single-AZ placement removes the cross-AZ charge and reintroduces exactly the failure mode multi-AZ exists to prevent — and a zone failure is a real event with a real frequency, not a theoretical one. Any design where a single AZ outage takes the service down has traded a modest recurring cost for an occasional total outage, which is almost never the right side of that trade.

The version that works is zone-aware routing without zone-pinned placement: replicas in every AZ so failure is survivable, but a preference for a same-zone endpoint when one is healthy. Kubernetes calls this topology-aware routing and meshes call it locality-weighted load balancing; both fall back across zones when local endpoints are unhealthy, giving single-AZ cost with multi-AZ availability. That answer is worth giving because it declines the false choice in the question.

The genuine exceptions are non-critical, high-volume flows: batch processing, log shipping, analytics pipelines and anything asynchronous with a retry path. Pinning those to one AZ is a legitimate saving with a bounded consequence, and it is where the real money usually is anyway.

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The mechanism is billing rather than protocol; the arithmetic below discharges this section, and the boundaries themselves are covered in Items 122–129.

The stacking arithmetic is the point. Consider one gigabyte from a private subnet to a vendor API, with a single shared NAT gateway in another AZ and a Transit Gateway hub. That gigabyte is charged: cross-AZ out plus cross-AZ in to reach the gateway, Transit Gateway data processing, NAT gateway data processing, and internet egress — five charges on one gigabyte. Moving the NAT gateway into the same AZ removes two; giving the VPC local egress removes a third. None of those changes are visible on the architecture diagram, and all of them are route table edits.

The Kubernetes multiplier is the one people miss. In a three-AZ cluster with zone-agnostic Service routing, the probability that a randomly chosen pod-to-pod call stays in-zone is about 1/3, so roughly two thirds of all internal traffic is charged cross-AZ in both directions. For a microservice architecture where a single user request fans out to a dozen internal calls, that multiplies quickly — and the traffic is invisible at the perimeter, so it never appears in any capacity model.

The remedy hierarchy follows the arithmetic. Eliminating a meter beats reducing bytes: a free gateway endpoint removes two charges outright, which no compression matches. Then localisation — same-AZ, same-region — and only then volume reduction. Teams usually attempt these in reverse order, which is why the effort-to-saving ratio disappoints.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

(Read as: when cost optimisation here is the wrong move.)

  • Do not collapse to a single AZ to save transfer costs on a critical path. You have exchanged a predictable recurring cost for an unpredictable total outage, and the fix — zone-aware routing with multi-AZ placement — gets most of the saving with none of the risk.

  • Do not centralise egress purely for cost without doing the arithmetic. Centralisation removes hourly charges and adds a per-GB hub charge; for a few very high-volume VPCs that is a net loss.

  • Do not chase compression and batching before eliminating meters. A free gateway endpoint removes 100% of two charges; a compression project removes perhaps 70% of one.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "Traffic inside a VPC is free."

✅ Reality: Traffic inside a VPC and inside one AZ, over private addresses, is free. Cross the AZ boundary and it is charged per gigabyte in both directions — and in a multi-AZ Kubernetes cluster, most internal traffic does exactly that by default.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "One NAT gateway is the cheap option."

✅ Reality: It saves two hourly charges and adds cross-AZ transfer on roughly two thirds of all egress, in both directions, on top of NAT processing. Beyond a few hundred gigabytes a month it costs more than the gateways it replaced — while also making one zone a dependency for every VPC's internet access.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)

  • 124-igw-nat-egress.md — the NAT and internet meters, in mechanism form

  • 129-privatelink-vpc-endpoints.md — the free and cheap alternatives to the NAT path

  • 123-subnets-azs-cidr-planning.md — the AZ boundary that all of this is priced around

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

  • 135-multi-region-networking.md — where cross-region transfer becomes the dominant term

  • 128-transit-gateway.md — a hub's per-GB charge against its hourly savings

  • Section 11 119-cdn-and-edge.md — moving bytes off the origin egress path entirely

headings.text: Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)
Why can't a service in one region simply call a database in another?
Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)
Active-active or active-passive?
⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)
⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Health-based regional failover — AWS: Failover routing (Route 53)

  • Active-active versus active-passive, as the provider models them — AWS: Active-active and active-passive failover

  • Latency-based regional selection — AWS: Values specific for latency records

  • Bonus — AWS: Overview of Data Transfer Costs for Common Architectures

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What is the hard part of multi-region? Not the network — it is the data. Networking is a weekend; consistency is the project.
Realistic DNS failover time? Minutes: health-check detection plus TTL plus caches that ignore it (Section 11, Item 115).
What does data residency constrain? Where data may be stored and processed — which forecloses "just route to the nearest region".
Active-active's hidden cost? Cross-region replication traffic, charged per GB, plus conflict resolution you now own.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Multi-region is three separate problems that get discussed as one. Routing — sending a user to a region — is solved by latency-based or health-based DNS, or by anycast at an edge tier. Latency is physics: 70 to 250 milliseconds between distant regions, which forbids synchronous cross-region calls on a request path. Data is the hard part: active-passive means a replica and a failover procedure, active-active means write conflicts and a consistency model you have to choose. Networking is the easy third, which is why a design that only covers routing has not answered the question.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

Why can't a service in one region simply call a database in another?

Because the round trip is 70 to 250 milliseconds depending on the region pair, and that cost is paid per call, not per request. A request that makes eight sequential database calls — entirely ordinary — turns a 400-millisecond cross-region round-trip budget into three and a half seconds of pure network time, before any query executes. Latency between regions is a physical constraint set by the speed of light in fibre plus routing overhead; no provider feature reduces it.

The architectural consequence is that each region must be able to serve its traffic without synchronous dependencies on another. That means region-local reads, region-local caches, and any cross-region communication being asynchronous — replication, event streams, batch. A design where region B's application calls region A's database has not built two regions; it has built one region with a remote frontend, and it will be slower than the single-region version it replaced.

The second consequence is that a partial multi-region deployment is often worse than none. Failing over compute to a second region while the database stays in the first gives you every millisecond of cross-region latency and none of the availability benefit, because the surviving region still depends on the failed one.

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

Active-active or active-passive?

🎯 Really testing: whether you price the operational cost of conflict resolution honestly, rather than treating active-active as strictly better.

Active-passive keeps one region authoritative and replicates asynchronously to a standby. Consistency is simple because there is one writer; the costs are a recovery point objective greater than zero — whatever is in flight at failure is lost — a recovery time set by DNS propagation plus promotion, and a standby that is either idle and wasteful or scaled down and unproven. The classic failure is discovering during an incident that the standby was never load-tested at full traffic.

Active-active serves from both regions and removes the failover step entirely, at the price of concurrent writes to the same logical data. You now need a conflict model: partitioning by tenant or geography so writes never collide, last-writer-wins with its silent data loss, or CRDTs and application-level merge logic. Cross-region replication traffic is charged per gigabyte in both directions, and it is continuous rather than incident-driven.

My default is active-passive with a regularly exercised failover, moving to active-active only when the driver is genuine — a latency requirement that a single region cannot meet for a global user base, or a residency rule that forces data to stay in-region. The strongest version of active-active is the one that avoids the conflict problem by construction: partition users by home region so each record has exactly one writer, which gives you active-active's latency and availability without its consistency work. If you cannot partition, be honest that you are signing up for conflict resolution as a permanent engineering commitment.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Single region Active-passive Active-active, partitioned Active-active, shared writes
Failover time n/a — outage Minutes (DNS + promotion) Seconds to none None
Data loss on failure n/a Whatever was in flight Only the failed partition's tail Depends on the conflict model
Consistency work None None — one writer None — one writer per partition Substantial and permanent
Cross-region traffic cost None Replication only Replication + some cross-partition Continuous, both directions
Standby confidence n/a Low unless exercised High — it serves real traffic High
When you'd actually pick it Most products, most of the time A real availability or DR requirement Global users with a natural partition key Only when nothing else fits

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The latency budget is the constraint that shapes everything. Inter-region round trips run from roughly 70 milliseconds for nearby pairs to 250 or more for antipodal ones, set by fibre distance rather than by provider engineering. A request that makes n sequential cross-region calls costs n × RTT in network time alone, so the only viable pattern is one cross-region hop per request at most, and preferably none.

Failover time is a sum, not a TTL. Real recovery is health-check detection (interval × threshold) plus DNS TTL plus downstream caches that do not honour it plus database promotion time. A "60-second TTL" system realistically moves most traffic in two to five minutes with a long tail — which is why an availability target tighter than that cannot rest on DNS failover alone and needs anycast or an always-warm second path (Section 11, Item 115).

Replication lag sets the recovery point objective. Asynchronous replication means the standby is behind by the lag at the moment of failure, so the data loss window is the replication lag — which makes lag a first-class monitored metric rather than a database detail, and makes a lag spike an availability event even while everything is healthy.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Do not go multi-region for availability before exhausting multi-AZ. Multi-AZ handles the failure mode that actually occurs most often, costs a fraction as much, and requires no consistency work. A full region outage is rare; a design that cannot survive an AZ loss is the more urgent problem.

  • Do not split compute across regions while the data stays in one. Every cross-region call pays the full round trip and the surviving region still depends on the failed one — worse latency and no availability gain.

  • Do not build active-active without a partition key. Shared concurrent writes commit you to conflict resolution forever; if users, tenants or geographies give you a natural home region, use it and avoid the problem entirely.

  • Do not treat a passive region as ready because it exists. An untested standby is a hypothesis. Scheduled failover exercises are what convert it into a capability, and they are the part that gets cut.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "Multi-region is mostly a networking problem."

✅ Reality: The networking is the easy part — DNS routing and inter-region connectivity are a small amount of configuration. The work is in the data layer: replication topology, consistency model, conflict handling and failover procedure, none of which the network layer touches.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "Lowering the DNS TTL gives us fast regional failover."

✅ Reality: TTL is one term in a sum that also includes health-check detection, resolver and client caches that ignore your TTL, and database promotion. Dropping the TTL from 300 to 30 seconds improves a number that was never the dominant one, and the tail of clients pinned to the failed region persists for far longer than any TTL suggests.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)

  • 122-vpc-mental-model.md — regions and the boundaries between them

  • Section 11 115-global-load-balancing.md — the routing half, in mechanism form

  • 01-mental-models/08-speed-of-light-budget.md — why inter-region latency is not negotiable

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

  • 134-egress-cost-data-transfer.md — cross-region transfer, usually the dominant cost term here

  • 136-network-security-posture.md — residency requirements as a security and compliance constraint

  • CAP, replication and consistency in the System Design folder — the half this note deliberately does not cover

Why is the instance metadata service a security concern, and what does v2 fix?
Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)
How much egress filtering is worth the operational cost?
⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)
⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • IMDSv2 and why the session-token handshake matters — AWS: Use the Instance Metadata Service to access instance metadata

  • Enforcing v2 across a fleet — AWS: Transition to using Instance Metadata Service Version 2

  • The credentials that make the metadata service a target — AWS: Retrieve security credentials from instance metadata

  • Bonus — AWS: Ensure internetwork traffic privacy in Amazon VPC

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What address is the metadata service on? 169.254.169.254 — link-local, unroutable, and reachable from any process on the host.
What does IMDSv2 change? A PUT session-token handshake with a hop limit — which defeats SSRF and container escape by default.
What does egress filtering need that NAT cannot give? Hostname visibility. NAT sees addresses; only a proxy sees which host was called.
What does "private-only" actually mean? No route to an internet gateway anywhere, and managed services reached via endpoints.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Network security posture in the cloud is four decisions. Private-only workloads: nothing sits in a subnet with an internet gateway route unless it must be reachable. Egress filtering: outbound is an allow-list at hostname granularity, which requires a proxy, because NAT only sees addresses. Zero-trust between services: identity rather than network location decides access, which means security groups referencing groups, and mTLS or NetworkPolicy inside clusters. And IMDSv2 enforced everywhere, because the metadata service hands out role credentials to anything that can make an HTTP request from the host — which an SSRF bug can.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

Why is the instance metadata service a security concern, and what does v2 fix?

🎯 Really testing: whether you can name the attack chain, not just the setting.

The metadata service lives at the link-local address 169.254.169.254 and, among other things, returns temporary credentials for the instance's IAM role. Any process on the host can fetch them with an unauthenticated GET, which is the design — that is how the SDK obtains credentials without a secret on disk. The problem is that "any process" includes anything an attacker can induce to make a request.

The classic chain is server-side request forgery: an application feature that fetches a user-supplied URL is pointed at 169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/, and the response — real, usable credentials — comes back in the application's own output. No code execution required. The 2019 Capital One breach is the widely-documented instance of exactly this shape, and it is why the topic sits in a networking note rather than an application-security one: the boundary that failed was a network-reachable address, not a permission.

IMDSv2 closes it with a session-oriented handshake: the caller must first issue a PUT to obtain a token, then present that token on subsequent requests. That defeats SSRF because the vulnerable feature almost always performs a GET and cannot be coerced into a PUT with custom headers. It also enforces a hop limit on the response's IP TTL — set to 1, the response cannot leave the host, so a container using the default bridged networking cannot reach it either, which incidentally closes the container-escape variant. Enforcing HttpTokens: required on every launch template is the control; leaving v1 optional means the old path still works.

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

How much egress filtering is worth the operational cost?

📍 Seen in the wild: the follow-up on any AI-platform design once agents can call arbitrary APIs.

🎯 Really testing: whether you distinguish workloads by how predictable their destinations are.

For a service with a fixed, small set of dependencies, an allow-list is cheap and durable: a handful of hostnames, changed when a dependency is added, with a proxy in the path that costs a hop. The operational burden is real but bounded, and the audit value is immediate.

For workloads whose destinations are dynamic by design — CI runners executing third-party code, or agents calling tools chosen by a model — the calculus inverts. There is no fixed list to maintain, so the allow-list becomes a per-tenant policy surface that changes constantly, and every addition is a decision someone must make quickly or the product breaks. That is genuinely expensive. It is also the case where filtering matters most, because the destination set is chosen by something you do not control, and the alternative is an audit answer of "we don't know".

My position: hostname allow-listing through a forward proxy for anything that executes untrusted or model-directed code, accepting the operational cost as the price of being able to answer the exfiltration question. For ordinary services, a proxy with a permissive default and full logging gets most of the audit value at a fraction of the burden — you can answer what was called even if you did not block it. What is never acceptable is treating a NAT gateway as the control, because its flow logs record addresses and a CDN-hosted destination is indistinguishable from any other tenant of that CDN.

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

Defence in depth here is a chain, and each link has a distinct blind spot. Private subnets remove the inbound path but do nothing about a compromised process inside. Security groups express identity-based policy but stop at the node boundary for most container networking. Endpoint policies restrict which resources may be reached but only for AWS services. A forward proxy sees hostnames but not payloads. IMDSv2 protects credentials but nothing else. The posture is the composition, and naming what each layer cannot see is what distinguishes an architecture answer from a checklist.

The exfiltration path worth tracing explicitly runs: compromised workload → outbound connection → destination. Security groups can restrict outbound by address, which a dynamic destination defeats; endpoint policies can restrict S3 to your own buckets, which closes the most common bulk-data path; a proxy allow-list closes the rest at hostname granularity. Leave all three permissive and the answer to "what left" is a NAT flow log full of CDN addresses.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Do not rely on network controls for policy that belongs to identity. A compromised workload has the network access its legitimate self had; IAM scope, short-lived credentials and least privilege limit the damage in ways no route table can.

  • Do not treat NAT flow logs as an egress audit. They record addresses and byte counts. "Did this workload call an unapproved API" is unanswerable from them once destinations are behind shared CDN ranges.

  • Do not assume security groups isolate pods. For most CNIs they apply at the node interface, so pod-to-pod traffic within a node is unfiltered by them entirely; NetworkPolicy or a mesh authorization policy is the control that reaches there.

  • Do not leave IMDSv1 enabled because "nothing uses v2 yet". Modern SDKs negotiate v2 automatically, the transition is a launch template setting plus a fleet audit, and the exposure it leaves open is credential theft from a bug class that appears in ordinary application code.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "Workloads in private subnets can't be reached, so they're safe."

✅ Reality: Private subnets remove the inbound path. Every serious cloud compromise of the last decade went the other direction — a vulnerability in an application that was reachable by design, followed by outbound access that nothing constrained. Egress is the half that gets neglected and the half that is used.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "IMDSv2 is a hardening nice-to-have, like disabling a legacy protocol."

✅ Reality: It closes a complete, unauthenticated credential-theft path that a single SSRF bug in ordinary application code can walk. The attack needs no code execution, no privilege escalation and no lateral movement — one request to a link-local address returns usable role credentials. Enforcing v2 is one setting against one of the shortest attack chains in cloud computing.
